subsubtopic: PROPOSED CREATION OF FOOD MINISTRY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on an important and urgent matter.
In view of the increasingly obvious need for adopting clear and specific policies on the food sector which will again be affected this year by considerably higher costs and so affect Canadian consumers as well, and as the farming sector is up against certain difficulties including, for instance, an expected much lower farm income for the year in spite of relentlessly higher production costs, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House now study the recommendation made recently by the Food Prices Review Board for setting up at provincial and federal government levels a food ministry entrusted with the formulation of a coherent food policy, and that this House analyze any proposal of similar nature capable of ensuring balance between food production and food consumption, thus sparing all Canadians, producers and consumers, the consequences of the lack of planning in that sphere.

subtopic: REGULATIONS COVERING PEOPLE HANDLING FOOD IN RESTAURANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, Canada has a very extensive program of health screening of all immigrants coming into Canada, particularly with regard to contagious diseases. As a matter of fact, Canada has a more comprehensive program in that respect than the United States, Britain or France. Where the problem arises is in the case of non-immigrants, that is, people coming to Canada for short stays which, as the hon. member knows, number in the tens of millions every year. Both my department and the Department of Manpower and Immigration are currently looking at means whereby we can establish some kind of selective regulations. subsubtopic: HIDDEN RESERVES OF CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
The chartered banks and other businesses which extend credit are exposed to losses from bad or doubtful debts and to depreciation in the value of assets and maintain contingency reserves to meet such losses. The banks are permitted to set aside amounts from pre-tax earnings, within limits prescribed by the Minister of Finance which relate such amounts to the level of assets at risk, for the purpose of maintaining General Appropriations for Losses. Prior to the enactment of the present Bank Act at the time of the last decennial revision, the banks included such appropriations in their balance sheets as deductions from related assets. These deductions were frequently referred to as "hidden" or "inner" reserves. Since 1967 the banks have been required to disclose these reserves on the liability side of their balance sheets as "Accumulated Appropriations for Losses". Further disclosure is made through the Statement of Accumulated Appropriations for Losses which analyzes changes in the appropriations accounts. Since 1967 the permitted maximum of General, or pre-tax, Appropriations has been reduced twice. This has meant that, with few exceptions, the larger banks have not been able to add to their General Appropriations from pre-tax earnings. subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned the debate on this bill on Thursday I was addressing myself to the position taken by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt). Although I agree with the philosophy she expressed in her speech, I find it rather interesting, politically, that she should have compared the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) with Adolf Hitler. To the best of my knowledge, the Secretary of
(Mr. Blais.]
State has not taken up painting; but there may be other grounds for leading the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway to infer that there is more than a passing similarity between this legislation and legislation introduced by the Chancellor of Germany in the 1930s. Let me repeat in part what the hon. member said in the House last Thursday. As reported on page 11134 of Hansard, she said:
-The Secretary of State announced in committee that he had a cultural plan for Canada. That has happened before, with nationalism as the driving force, the most notable example being the German cultural plan announced in Mein Kampf by Adolf Hitler.
I think that for this House to consider the Secretary of State in that light is going a bit far. Of course, I must defer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway who has greater knowledge of the hon. gentleman than I have. I was impressed with the hon. member's quotation from Somerset Maugham. Referring to that writer, she said, as reported on page 11136 of Hansard:
If a nation values anything more than freedom, it will lose that freedom ... And the irony of it is that if it is money that is valued more than freedom, that too will be lost.
As I said on Thursday, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway expressed sincerely her feelings about freedom, truth and censorship. I think her feelings might involve her in further difficulty with the government, particularly if it persists in proceeding with this bill despite the opposition of my party, the opposition in the government party and the opposition in the country.
Parts of this bill offend both the print and electronic media, particularly that part of the electronic media in which current developments have come to a halt. One can hardly expect new owners of cablevision stations to invest money in what were hitherto money-makers if, under the new rules as adumbrated by Mr. Justice Dube, there will be no guarantee that the owners will retain their licences even if they conform with every last instruction of the CRTC-of which, heaven knows, there are enough instructions.
This government believes in confrontation. It is confronting a major industry of Canada with the idea that it, and it alone, knows what is best for Canadians to watch and to hear; that it, and it alone, can say how these businesses must be conducted. If there were a valuable mineral resource under some new town or under where a new town might be built or, say, under Kincaid, Saskatchewan, or under any other city built on the prairies, I would not give a nickel for the cablevision licence for that community under existing west coast rules affecting cablevision. All this means that capital investment and development will stop entirely. That will enable the government to move in and say that the private sector of the economy is not fulfilling its task, and take over cablevision stations that up to now have been flourishing.
To indicate the difficulties this government is creating for our industry, may I quote a short extract from a letter written by the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia. The letter has to do mainly with Time and Reader's Digest. I do not always agree with the council, but I must concede that it knows about the forest industry of British Columbia and the likely effects of this bill on that industry. The first paragraph reads:
February 23, 1976

-Bill C-58 could be harmful to our industry's market position in the United States. We urged the government to withdraw the bill and reconsider the position it had taken.
In the penultimate paragraph it states:
As a member representing a British Columbia constituency, you will be well aware of the dependence of this province's forest industry on the U.S. market. Our members are increasingly concerned that U.S./Canadian relations are deteriorating and that this trend may jeopardize access to our principal market.
I wish to say a few words about Canada-U.S. relations and how they are deteriorating. Bill C-58 is an added rough spot in our relations. We seem determined to keep these relations in constant friction. To take dead aim at something like Time magazine is a sure way of ensuring that we do not return to the more tranquil days that we had before this government took office. Conditions have steadily become worse.
When this bill was first introduced, we were given to understand that "not similar content" was 50 per cent different. This was accepted by the trade, the industry and the House, including several members of this party. Our first reaction was that the bill was not all that bad. The ministry then decided to up the ante. They went to 60 per cent. When they found this was not an absolute bar to these two publishers, they went to 80 per cent. I understand the minister said they would go higher, if necessary, to make certain that Time magazine did not manage to continue publishing in this country. This is a very strange attitude for a government to take, singling out a magazine like this, saying it is the wrong thing for our innocent people to be reading. They say that if we prohibit their selling advertising to Canadians as a normal Canadian business expense, everyone will turn to read Maclean's magazine.
Last week I spoke for a few minutes about Maclean's magazine. That was the previous issue. I now have the February 23 issue: that is very fast delivery. I wish to tell hon. members about this magazine that is supposed to replace Time as a news magazine. As I stated last week, I am particularly interested in the foreign affairs section. This week's cover does not have a picture of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The only similarity is that it looks like a mad scientist or doctor who bears resemblance to the Secretary of State.
The world news begins on page 37. Last week there were three pages. This week there are two articles in what is supposed to be a news magazine. In fact, it states on the front page, "Canada's Newsmagazine". The first is an article on Lockheed. It is headed, "The Lockheed revelations imperil the Dutch Monarchy". That is current. I wish to read a paragraph from the article:
Considering the global scope of Lockheed's pay-offs, it wasn't surprising that Canadian plans to spend $950 million for 18 Lockheed Orion long-range aircraft were frozen pending the outcome of emergency talks between defence minister James Richardson and the U.S. aircraft manufacturer. There were fears that Lockheed might not be able to complete the deal although Richardson stressed there was "no question" of any Canadian official being involved in the scandal.
The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) said that was not the case. He said the only problem was long-term financing. It is nice to see Canada mentioned as a country of the world, but the story does not quite give
Non-Canadian Publications
the picture of actual events. The second article is, "Leonid Brezhnev: a plodder's progress". It is a laudable article on Brezhnev. However, that is all the world news: there is nothing other than articles on Lockheed and the dictator of Russia. There is an enchanting article about young people. It concerns the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery). This is typical of what we will have to get used to if we are to have Maclean's as our news magazine. It states that the hon. member for Spadina has been moonlighting as a part-time cab driver. I admire him for this activity. He is getting out to meet the people. Another quote with which I agree, and the hon. member must have said this to the reporter because it is in quotes, is as follows:
"You get disconnected in Ottawa," he says. "Cab driving teaches you the value of a dollar."
I suggest that the entire front bench take up cab driving to learn the value of a dollar.
"They don't have a sense of value here (in Ottawa). They don't know what a dollar is."
That is true. However, it then goes on with typical Maclean's slush. It refers to the hon. member taking a January walking trip to Central America's mosquito coast, and visits to the close friend who works for France's distinguished Folies Bergere. The article concludes:
"In Ottawa," he complains, "all you can do in winter is skate and that'll freeze your ass off."
That is the kind of cute article Maclean's likes to publish. It makes a Liberal look favourable and then ends up with a crude expression. This is one reason that magazine is unable to compete with Time as far as readership in Canada is concerned. I wish to quote from a couple of letters I have received from constituents who are concerned that they will not be able to continue buying and enjoying their favourite magazine. The first is from a doctor. It reads:
Dear Sir:
As my only direct representative in our federal government, I am appealing to you to use your utmost effort to oppose the government's intention to amend the Income Tax Act, which may very seriously affect the Canadian edition of the Reader's Digest.
1 have been a constant reader of this magazine for over 25 years, and have always considered it to be primarily Canadian, as opposed to any other foreign publication. During these years I have had occasion, for somewhat extended periods, to read the English edition. No one would say that this was an "American" magazine any more than the Canadian edition is in that category.
Quite apart from the impressive statistics of the contribution to the economic and cultural life of Canada which the Reader's Digest has contributed, surely the impetus of the hundreds of thousands of readers can only further emphasize its importance in Canada. No other Canadian magazine can take its place or even compete with its worldwide spectrum of interest.
I urge you to use your best judgment, your demonstrated fairness and persuasive powers to defeat this discriminatory legislation.
Yours sincerely, Moreley R. Elliott, M.D.
P.S. The almost identical argument is applicable to the iconoclastic proposals re the Canadian edition of Time magazine.
I should like now to read from another letter. This comes from a place called Rose Manor, in Victoria. Rose Manor is a home for aged ladies. This is the kind of dear soul you

February 23, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
find so often in our constituency. The letter is addressed to me, and it reads:
Dear Sir:
I am writing in protest against the proposed revision of the Income Tax Act and asking you as my representative to vote against it. The bill has nothing to recommend it but the very unlikely prospect of diverting tax money from one magazine to others in an effort to assist the development of a domestic news magazine and to foster national integrity and self-expression. The Reader's Digest does not interfere in any way in this worthy object. It is undemocratic and unjust to discriminate against one firm because it attracts more advertisers, and to use dictatorship against millions of Canadians who admire the uniqueness of this magazine and enjoy reading it. Anyone has the right to compete with it if they wish.
The public is ignored completely. Have we no rights under this government? I am nearly 90 years old and one of the few pleasures I have left is reading something worth while. It is not right to put hundreds of Canadians out of work and to deprive Canada of millions of dollars in revenue. I urge you and all fair-minded people not to allow this bill to pass.
Sincerely, (Mrs.) Caroline Barber.
I should like to read one paragraph from another letter I have received:
Please leave it as it is. It is clean, informative, full of local and international news. I know of no competition to it.
That is the thread which runs through my mail. Letter after letter tells me it is a favourite magazine which my correspondents would not know how to replace because they can find nothing in Canadian periodicals which is equivalent or which they really want to read. The harm which the bill would do to the Canadian economy should by now be apparent to all. Even so, the $30 million loss to the economy which would result if this bill were passed has not in my view been sufficiently emphasized. The publishing operation would, of course, go back to the United States, and postage on copies ordered would have to be paid by Canadians. Consequently, the money paid as postage for these magazines would be a direct loss to the Canadian government. I am greatly surprised that the present administration, of all governments, would wish to countenance a loss of revenue.
In closing, let me say this. Long ago there were two cities in ancient Greece-Sparta and Athens. Sparta was a commercial success, a militaristic dictatorship. Athens was a city where great attention was paid to culture. All the cultures of the ancient world were welcomed there. The educational institutions were the finest in the world. Today, Athens is visited by millions of travellers from every country who come to see the place where the free society of Athens raised monuments of such beauty in the way of statuary, architecture and tradition. It is still the envy of the rest of the world. By contrast, Sparta, which concentrated on other things, is hard to find: just a few hummocks on the ground is all that is left of a nation which neglected to pay attention to its culture, which tried to seal its people off from the rest of the world and keep them in isolation so that no comparison could be made between their nation and other nations. I believe Canada would prefer to choose the way of Athens rather than the way of Sparta. I urge all hon. members to support this amendment and to send the bill back to committee so as to allow much needed revisions to be made to it at that time.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of entering the debate today. I do so because I have been tremendously concerned about the attitude which has been taken with respect to Bill C-58. Right from the introduction of this measure, or shortly thereafter, we became aware of the direction in which we were going, a direction very much in opposition to the one in which we felt the government should be moving at this time.
I pointed out at a previous stage of the debate that the government have constantly engaged in confrontation. It does not seem to matter what area they are dealing with; they are so confident they are right and that everyone else is wrong that they have never hesitated to use extraordinary means by which to maintain their point of view. This has been the case as far as Bill C-58 is concerned.
In the earlier stages of our discussion, as I am sure the country is aware, a great deal of attention was paid to representations which we had received from the people of Canada. I suppose every member of the House has received a great many communications calling attention to the fact that what the government was doing was not in the best interests of the country and, moreover, that it was contrary to the wishes of the Canadian people. It was made clear that the end result of the program in which the government was engaged would be a serious interference with the rights of citizens of this country to read what they wanted to read and not to be circumscribed in the material available to them.
As far as Reader's Digest is concerned, a great many members, including myself, have pointed out that this magazine is welcomed in most homes across the nation. It is informative, it is entertaining, it is a wholesome magazine, one we are not ashamed to leave on the table in our living room for anyone who enters to pick up and read- and that is something we hesitate to do with some of the periodicals which are published right here in Canada. I do not think we can take the attitude that anything which is printed or owned in Canada is a good magazine or a good periodical, nor can we take the position that what is published outside our borders is wrong or unsuitable.
For all these reasons, I believe we need to take a further hard look at this legislation. If the government will not do so, the opposition will, very possibly, have to carry on until members opposite understand the situation. It seems to me beyond reason that the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) should take the position he is taking, determined to have his own way even though members of his own party stand and take exception to it. His own friends draw attention to the dangers that are involved, and ask him, in the name of common sense, to bring in changes to the legislation. As I say, it is almost beyond my understanding that the minister should refuse, even if he will not listen to members of the opposition, to accept the arguments of his own supporters with regard to what we believe is the right of Canadians to read whatever they wish.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I felt I had to stand and reaffirm my position on this measure. I had the opportunity of speaking on one of the motions introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) and also on some of the
February 23, 1976

motions introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen). Here, again, I believe their arguments were appropriate; they were direct, sane and sensible. It almost appears as if the minister is not willing to look at things that are sane and sensible, but is determined to pursue the course he has outlined regardless of the consequences or its effect on this country.
I do not believe we have the right to say, "This is the course we are going to take regardless of any other considerations. It is going to be this way, or none". Several years ago, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was minister of justice, he said-I cannot quote his exact words, but this is the gist of his message-that he looked upon his responsibility as minister of justice not only as being legal adviser to the government but as charting a course for Canadian society. I suggest that is exactly what he has been trying to do. There were those who at that time said he was just trying to find his way. I replied that he was not trying to find his way, that he knew where he wanted to go and was going there. We now have the Secretary of State following that course and supplementing the program that has been announced by saying, "As far as Canadian culture is concerned, this will be it, regardless what the people of Canada think about it. We are going this way, and they can like it or lump it". That position is entirely out of order as far as I am concerned.
Reader's Digest is a magazine that was greatly in the forefront of the discussions that were taking place. We now know that some changes were made. In some way the government and Reader's Digest came to the understanding that they would be able to continue to publish. I do not think the minister has ever outlined to us just what was said or what kind of agreement was reached. I think I ought also to say that while Reader's Digest was very definitely desirous of placing their arguments and the basis for their complaints before us, I do not think they did a very good job of coming back to us and saying, "Well, you fellows put up a pretty good fight, but now we want to tell you what the situation is". It seems to me that if the government will not tell us, Reader's Digest ought to state what the situation is and how they were able to fit in with the plan the government outlined.
We are glad that Reader's Digest will be able to continue publication. I like to have it in my home and I like to read it. Some say that it is not very deep. Just because it is not very deep is not to say that it is not enlightening, informative and pleasant reading. As I have said, I like Reader's Digest and I want it in my home, and I would like to know the basis of the understanding that was reached between the government and that magazine.
Some attention had been give the matter of the "80 per cent difference" provision. This seems to me a mysterious situation. In order to reinforce the position of the government, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) warned the industry, "If you don't measure up, or if you find some loophole to get past, we will soon introduce more legislation so you won't get past". It seems to me absolutely preposterous that a government should take this position regarding legislation presented to the House, legislation that has been opposed by members of the opposition as well as supporters of the government.
Non-Canadian Publications
We have before us a measure that has eliminated Time magazine. Here, again, if people want to read Time magazine and have a Canadian section in it, I cannot see why in the world they should not have the privilege of doing so. But, again, the axe has fallen. We are now finding other so-called Canadian magazines moving in which have no appeal at all to the broad mass of the Canadian people, yet hope to take over the market occupied by Time magazine. They will not be able to do it unless they come up with something vastly different from what they have at the present time.
I have spoken about the printed materials that are affected by this particular measure, and I should now like to turn to its effect on the television industry and on Canadian culture. Canadian culture is a relative thing. What the Secretary of State would call Canadian culture, other people would call garbage, and perhaps vice versa.

speechtext: Only Tories.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
No; what about your own supporters? The minister does not have his ears and eyes open; he cannot see or understand. His mind is fixed on, "Come what may, you are going to do it my way." That seems to me to be a blatant disregard of the rights of the Canadian people. A rather disturbing attitude seems to prevail among most members on the government side-though, thank goodness, not all-when we begin talking about Canadian culture and foreign influence. The attitude seems to be that if something has a Canadian designation, however superficial, it has to be good; it is worthy of our acclaim and should be revered. This attitude is seen very clearly in a statement made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) some time ago and in the position she took regarding KVOS. The inference is that any group or letter designating a Canadian broadcasting licence automatically makes a TV station a better one.
I suggest that that is not so. I think the essential point in any discussion about KVOS-which is a station that has wide support in my area of the country-one upon which any decision should be predicated, is that KVOS is not just another foreign television station serving Canadian markets. KVOS has-in my analysis of the facts, at least- tried to observe the norms of good corporate Canadian citizenship for more than 20 years. To return to the periodicals, Reader's Digest has been a good corporate citizen, employing a great number of Canadian people. It pays its taxes, enters into the Canadian economy and has made a tremendous contribution. Yet the government says, "That is not good enough. We don't want you here".
KVOS, as I was saying, Mr. Speaker, has tried to observe the norms of good corporate Canadian citizenship for more than 20 years. I wonder whether any hon. member can, or would, say as much about the CBC television network. I, for one, feel that some of the trash that has been broadcast by this TV network, which has more than enough Canadian-designated communication letters to satisfy hon. members representing the government from various parts, indicates that the CBC is not a good citizen at all. Its broadcasting often violates the norms of Canadian society, it offends the sensibilities of vast numbers of Canadian

February 23, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
people, and its slant on news stories and other social issues does more to undermine and destroy Canadian values, beliefs and objectives than to support them. The record of objections raised about CBC programming by hon. members in the House will serve as ample evidence of what I am saying. I can find no record of complaint by anyone against offensive material being carried on KVOS. Good corporate citizenship, then, involves considerably more than paying taxes and balancing the books-and those are items the CBC cannot even come close to achieving.
KVOS does pay Canadian income tax in Canada on its Canadian advertising sales and on its revenue from film production. The income of KVOS-TV, B.C., Ltd., is taxed equally by the Canadian and United States governments. Under an agreement between Canadian and U.S. tax authorities similar to that applying to the Canadian radio stations in Windsor serving the Detroit market, 50 per cent of the advertising dollars from Canadian national and retail advertisers becomes a commission revenue for KVOS-TV, B.C., Ltd., and 50 per cent is paid to KVOS-TV Incorporated, U.S., for supplying the on-the-air product to the Canadian corporation. None of the revenue produced by the two KVOS western film corporations, Canawest Film Productions Ltd., Vancouver, and Canawest Master Films, Calgary, goes to KVOS-TV, U.S.A., and tax thereon is therefore paid entirely to the Canadian government.
KVOS-TV, B.C., Ltd., is a Canadian corporation and employs Canadian workers. It pays Canadian taxes and also owns and operates the two aforementioned film companies. These two companies represent, together, the largest full-time film production unit west of Toronto. Approximately 30 full-time persons are employed by KVOS-TV, B.C., Ltd., and its production companies. Depending on production business and schedules, as many as 150 Canadian performers, artists, technicians, salesmen and office workers receive professional income from KVOS-TV at one time. In addition, KVOS invests a substantial amount of its profits in Canada and Canadian enterprise. For example, it has built and subsidizes a very successful film industry in British Columbia and Alberta. It has to date invested a significant amount of money, approximately $3 million, in both short-term and long-term Canadian securities. I could give other examples, but suffice it to say that from 1965 to 1974-nine years-KVOS-TV's contribution to the Canadian economy, the public and private sectors, has been $75,862,000.
I should like to list a number of other significant items that show the essential good citizen character of this corporation. KVOS voluntarily adheres to Canadian advertising regulations. This has been the case in respect of the proportion of commercials per hour in children's programs. KVOS did not wait for the regulations to be changed, but as soon as notification was received from the CRTC the change was voluntarily implemented. KVOS-TV has for 20 years voluntarily followed all restrictions that Canadian-based stations have in the broadcast treatment of Canadian elections and election news. When writing for and/or filming commercials for Canadian or Canadian-distributed products or services, both federal and provincial laws, regulations and codes are adhered to.
I could go on talking about KVOS, but I think this is sufficient to show that this organization is a good corpo-

rate citizen, just the same as Reader's Digest was, yet it seems as though it is to be given the axe. The result is that it is going to be in a very difficult situation as far as further contributions to the Canadian economy are concerned.
One suggestion made by KVOS was directed toward what apparently is one of the foremost concerns of the CRTC, and that is how to improve the quantity and quality of Canadian-made programs. More specifically, the offer of KVOS dealt with how to continue to build and strengthen production facilities in the west. KVOS made a submission to the CRTC to pay a percentage of its gross revenue to finance a western Canadian television fund. If the fund had been instituted as suggested, by the end of 1975 KVOS-TV, B.C., Ltd., alone would have advanced well over $1 million toward expending the film and television production industry in British Columbia.
I do not feel I should pursue this particular thought any further, although I certainly could. I have ample data which would enable me to continue to impress upon the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) the reasons this bill should be withdrawn, looked at again and amended. However, my hopes are not very high. I think the attitude of the minister has been shown very clearly. He is just going to sit it out and say, "When those people stop talking and yacking, then we are going to get this bill through and it will become the law of Canada." That is the attitude and reputation the minister has displayed and developed. He does not give a hoot about anybody else but his own program, and he is going to get it through.
I believe this bill should be the subject of another thorough examination. It should go back to the committee. Many of the things said in the committee have gone out the window now because of the deal made with Reader's Digest. This House has the absolute right to know just what happened and what took place before it gives approval to this measure or lets it go through this House.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments in respect of Bill C-58 at this stage. I realize that comments by hon. members on this side have been viewed with some degree of criticism by the minister responsible for the bill. I had hoped that this stage of the debate might have enlightened colleagues on all sides of the House about something that disturbs me. This has been mentioned by some of my colleagues as a question of privilege. I refer to the matter of closure of discussion in the committee and the fact that the whip was heavily applied to those members of the Liberal party who had expressed divergent views on the subject. I also hoped it would be possible to expose and identify the back room dealers and those deals which took place behind closed doors as a late stage when it was decided to treat Time and Reader's Digest differently.
The government almost paid the political price of obscuring this window to the world. The minister will recall that in my first speech I pleaded with him to make a distinction between Time and Reader's Digest. I had hoped this debate would give us the opportunity of finding out what went on behind closed doors that made it possible for the minister to change his mind and examine again the new information which obviously would have been before him at that time.
February 23, 1976

We are now faced with a different definition for a news magazine and a digest. It is now no longer sinful to bring in literary compositions from the outside, but it is sinful to bring in so-called general news. I suppose Time magazine could be called a news magazine. I suppose it is now bad for Canadians to read news coming in from other parts of the world.
My colleague, the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Patterson), who just spoke got the minister a little excited when he said that Canadians at times express concern over the cultural evolution that has been set up for some years through a type of closure which the CBC and the intellectual elitists are directing at Canadians. The minister said that it is only the Tories that are excited. What he meant was that only Canadians are excited, that the elitist group fully understand what is happening, is fully in accord with it and that, of course, they know better. The minister is saying, in effect, that the cultural evolution within our country must be directed, and it is not any longer the right of the individual taxpayer and citizen to express views in this regard.
I have always said that if the government wanted to clean up some of the mess which exists in respect of the newspaper, magazine and publications industry, it would do better if it would bring out some laws that would have the effect of cleaning up the magazine shelf itself. I respect the freedom of all Canadians, even those who like to read Playboy magazine and some of the other filth that is prominently displayed on the bookshelves. However, I would have thought the government would have made a greater contribution to a cultural evolution in our country by bringing in some directions concerning how some of these magazines, which some people find offensive, particularly when exposed to young people and children, should be displayed on the bookshelves. Some of my colleagues have referred to this matter and have alleged that the government's interest in all magazine content is coupled with just another tax law which is being used as part of an effort effectively to wipe out Time Canada.
I should like to address the House on a few specific points surrounding this bill with which I disagree. First let me point out that I hold no special affinity to the publication in question. I would make these comments regardless of the publication that might be concerned. It is, indeed, a sorry state of affairs when a country's laws are allowed to be distorted and aborted by bureaucratic redefinition. I fear this is merely the beginning and that it may become ingrained in our policies. The Liberals think that Canadians are not educated enough or astute enough to have the capability of discerning good from bad. That is what this bill implies. It is ludicrous for the government to believe the foolish notion that this country can be independent only if its publications are 80 per cent different from everyone else's publications. Its interest in editorial decisions is completely outside the law and is an area in which the government has no right or competence.
The desire to give fully-Canadian magazines a more prominent place in the publications business of Canada is commendable, but not at the expense of other magazines which have some redeeming value in this field. It is this kind of authoritarian rule which I fear. The government's
Non-Canadian Publications
desire to set itself above the publishing industry and to decide what constitutes an 80 per cent difference so as to allow tax deductions is a cheap form of pseudo censorship. The government is assuming editorial censorship. It is not doing so legitimately, because it could not be legitimized in any form. It is doing so, instead, by a new tax law-a roundabout way of meddling.
It will place hundreds of jobs in jeopardy if the publication in question succumbs. If the government fears that Time, Canada, is becoming a monopoly, perhaps the assets of Maclean-Hunter warrant a second look. Time, Canada, does not expect any special status and is willing to comply with every government demand except the "80 per cent different" rule. I suggest this might be for the reason that no one has ever defined what is meant by the "80 per cent different" rule. In a legal sense, this is without foundation on the part of the government.
If Time outsells Maclean's and Saturday Night, this is an indictment of our home-grown talent for its mediocrity. If they cannot compete on merit alone, they surely do not deserve to be protected through bullying on the part of politicians and bureacrats. That is obtuse thinking on the part of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner).
This insidious form of creeping censorship must be stopped in its tracks. It is a basic right of all Canadians to read what they choose. We are denying Canadians the right to read and view a full range of publications and programs. The effect of this policy scares me-not the stated intention of the Minister of National Revenue. It is a misconception to delude ourselves with the impression that lost revenue from advertising in Time will go to Canada's Maclean's. This is not the fact. The government says that if Canadians wish to read Time, let them get it from American sources. The crown of life is the exercise of choice. If we wish to read the magazine of our choice, that is our right and there is no reason we should have to pay a premium for that right. This is completely unfair and is no more than misplaced nationalism.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I wish to voice my disapproval over the deal this government made with Reader's Digest. The phrase "any type of continuing arrangement for access to material" is further proof that censorship is involved in this bill. I cannot agree with this interpretation which is completely unsubstantiated by statute and is only meant to run Time, Canada, out of this country.
Another magazine will be affected by Bill C-58. I should like to comment on that as well. The periodical to which I refer is MD of Canada. As I understand it, Bill C-58 is intended to strengthen the magazine industry in Canada. If MD of Canada is forced to discontinue publishing and distributing in Canada, nothing will be added to the objective of Bill C-58. MD of Canada competes with no other magazine of this nature. It is the only journal of its kind in Canada to begin with, so if it is removed, who will benefit? I am afraid that if it is removed, more will suffer as a result. MD of Canada is the only journal of medico-historical significance in this country that is distributed to physicians on a controlled basis.
MD of Canada has vindicated itself over the years. This is proven by the responses of physicians who receive it. Enrichment of the mind is surely the purpose of this

February 23, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
journal. From what I hear, MD has met this objective in the medical community. Further, MD is published, printed and edited in Canada and its contents are not duplicated in any other form in this country. To even consider relinquishing the distribution of this unique journal is a negative step. I suggest that the government re-evaluate what they are trying to do by imposing Bill C-58 on this publication.
I should like to make another brief point to do with the electronic media, particularly with regard to KVOS-TV in Vancouver. The government has clearly applied eastern regulations to a very specific and exceptional western situation. KVOS is indeed a good corporate citizen and always has been. It has proved itself more than adequate in the last 20 years. Furthermore, KVOS-TV has paid taxes to this government and it has received no carte blanche concessions, nor has it asked for any. For 20 years they have systematically reinvested substantial portions of their earnings into British Columbia and Alberta and have built in these two provinces the largest film production companies west of Toronto, with Canadian actors, writers, animators and production people of all kinds. They have done this to demonstrate good citizenship, and they have done it at a period of time when there was no competition and no one else to fill the void in Vancouver and in British Columbia.
Now that they have expanded their presence in Canada and have reinvested their profits in other industries, they stand accused of being a bunch of foreigners who are taking over this country. This company has diversified and invested its money in other industries, but the accusation is that they are engaging in a foreign take-over. They cannot win. The minister and the government are determined in any way possible to assume full control over the broadcasting industry in Canada, whether they are using bilingualism as an excuse, the government's intention to bring the French fact beyond a reversible position in Canada, the income tax laws, or whatever other excuse. They are determined to assume complete control of the broadcasting media in our country. That is frightening to most Canadians and, I suggest, to most of my colleagues in the House of Commons.
KVOS is entitled to a second look. I think we are being too hasty in writing it off, and especially in not analysing the KVOS offer put before the broadcasting committee which would repatriate a minimum of $2 million a year directly into British Columbia's broadcasting activities. KVOS has offered to share with CRTC all the profits. They are paying them out in taxes anyway, and they will have to lower their rates by 50 per cent if they want to stay in existence. They have offered to give CRTC 50 per cent of their profits after taxes, and will let CRTC direct this money into some form of broadcasting activity in our country. But this plea fell on deaf ears, and Canadians will be the poorer for it. In my opinion, this would better have met the objectives contained in Bill C-58 so far as British Columbia is concerned than the provisions of the bill at present. Just because there is a different problem in the west which could best be handled by applying a different solution, why should we be stuck with a national policy based on solving an eastern problem?

The government defends this invidious action by saying that the reason we must nationalize the broadcasting and magazine industries is that we have a responsibility to provide some form of news coverage and of cultural distribution to some of the more remote areas of our country, to Canada's hinterland, to mid-Canada and to northern Canada where we talk about the northern extension of the broadcasting system.
I live in the north and I live under regulations that CRTC brings out. As I have said before in the House of Commons, there would have been better ways of achieving the purposes of Bill C-58, particularly if CRTC were receptive to some ideas that come from the north and if some of the policies established by CRTC for itself could be amended to take into account and be more attuned to the needs of the north. I am making particular reference to one CRTC policy, namely, that if there is an area which has been identified as one which has only one national signal, either CTV or CBC, and some entrepreneur wanted to bring a cable program into the area, the CRTC would refuse the application for the simple reason that there is only one broadcasting signal in the area now.
I should like to ask the minister to consider the request which I have put forward on several occasions, to explain the reasoning behind that regulation which says that just because there is one signal or no signal at all in an area, they cannot get cablevision either. To me this does not make sense. I can identify several areas where this is happening. In the city of Prince George, with a population of 75,000, only last year CRTC allowed an application for cablevision because at that time one year had expired since the city had both CTV and CBC networks.
The same is true of the area of Skeena, Terrace and Kitimat-that great area in the province which my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo), represents. There is only one signal there. It happens to be CBC. Yet the CTV network had to sign an agreement with CRTC that eventually, over a reasonable period of time, their signal would have to be extended into the area. However, it is a five-year to ten-year program and until that time there can be no application for cablevision even in an area with a population of perhaps 80,000 to 100,000. They are denied cablevision programming because they do not have any other signal. The same is true of the Robson Valley area. There are not as many people there, but they had no television at all until a couple of years ago and CBC could not go in there because it would not be a paying proposition. So 7,500 people, in an area with a 200-mile radius, did not receive any kind of electronic programming. I admit they have radio, but there was no TV programming at all.
My predecessor in the House of Commons threw up his hands and said that CTV and CBC were prepared to look at the situation again in five years. I made a private deal with the telephone company in British Columbia which put up the tower and put in the signal and the facilities. We finally got CBC to pay an annual rent, because there was no money in the capital budget but lots of money in another budget, so we robbed Peter to pay Paul and we worked out an agreement under which CBC paid an annual rent. Now we have that one program in the area, but it will be many, many years before the other program
February 23, 1976

is put in there, because it is not a viable proposition in the area.
The same holds true of the Peace River country. As I go up the Alaska Highway, that storehouse of resources, that place where Canadians who still believe in the free enterprise system and in the spirit of individuality make their living and carve out their existence away from the concrete jungles, there is no television either. The reason there is no TV there is that CRTC would not ask a company such as KVOS if they would be prepared to spend some of their profits in such an area. They might have done it. Obviously, neither CBC or CTV do-because why should they? They have a captive audience now. They are in all the areas where profits are made, so why should they go up north? There is no competition in the city; it has all been chased out. Why should they go up north?
There is the other matter of saying that satellites are floating around and can be tracked with gadgets. I wrote to Japan about a metal shield that attracts a satellite. A kit is offered for $750 which can be operated in remote areas which have no electricity-although a little power plant is needed to run it. It is possible to pick up the signal from the satellite; but, Mr. Speaker, if you do that you go to jail. In the north, where there is no electricity and no programming, the satellite floats around, paid for by taxes generated in the north, but you cannot track it and put in your own broadcasting system.
Seventy-five miles from Prince George, which now has two signals and will have cablevision, is the town of Mackenzie. I met with the Chamber of Commerce there: they wanted to have the second signal. Some technicians said it would be a simple matter to hook up to it, and the way they explained it made sense. I suggested they should try it out. They took up a collection in town. That is the way they do things, Mr. Speaker. They are resourceful where I come from: they do not go running to the CRTC; they help themselves. If they want to skate, they flood an area at the back of the house. If they want to curl, they build themselves a rink. Sometimes they get a little LIP money. But they are resourceful people. So they climbed up a pole, hung on a reflector and, lo and behold, a beautiful signal appeared on the television screen.
They wanted to know what they would do then. I suggested they should leave the shield up there and enjoy the Saturday night hockey game. What did the minister do? He told them to take the thing down because they were not entitled to it without a licence. It could take a year of bureaucratic bungling to get a licence. First they had to hire an engineer, and then it became difficult. The engineer had to prove the system would work even though they already had a picture on the screen. He spent two or three months, and $20,000, to tell them the system would work. Now they can make their application to the CRTC because they have proof that it works.
As a representative of the north, am I amused when this kind of bill comes to the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker? No. I say it is high time we faced the problem as it exists- and that we all face it, not just the people on this side but the people responsible for the mess we are in.

Hear, hear!

speechtext: As it happens, KVOS was in Vancouver when programming in Vancouver was the way it is today in Dawson Creek. My hon. friend nods his head because he knows the problem is similar and I know he is working hard on it, too, but I should like him to compare the circumstances with Bill C-58-

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: Here comes the minister.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
KVOS was in Vancouver when things were like they are in Dawson Creek and in my hon. friend's constituency. Full service was not available at the time. The owners were American-but did they have two heads and seven arms? They were entrepreneurs coming to Canada . All their business was in Canada. Their production facilities were here and they hired Canadians living in Vancouver. There was a steel tower in Bellingham, just across the border, which was a convenient location from which to beam the signal into Vancouver. But that was all that was in the United States, except the owners.
I guess we have to make a decision whether to allow these bad people from the United States to influence our cultural evolution in this country. That is something members opposite have dreamed up with this legislation. The minister laughs, and if it were not so serious I could share his humour. But it really is not funny, Mr. Speaker, particularly when you examine Bill C-58 in light of what it means to KVOS in Vancouver and other entrepreneurs who have made a contribution to our way of life and are now penalized for it.
I have just returned from a trip to the United States where I had the honour of representing this parliament at an Interparliamentary Union meeting with the Congress of the United States. I have taken part in these meetings for the past three years. We discussed some of the irritants that have cropped up since the last meeting. There are always such things as border problems, waste being disposed of in the Great Lakes, the clean-up of the Great Lakes, the International Joint Commission, and such matters. On the agenda this year was Bill C-58. Mr. Speaker, I cannot put it any other way than to say I was ashamed. It was very, very difficult to defend what we are trying to do here, because I do not know what we are trying to do.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
We are called pirates. Our American colleagues look upon us as a banana republic. What we are doing with Bill C-58 will apply to other serious matters with the United States. There is the matter of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, for instance. One senator told me in private, "We might build a pipeline through your country, and we might put some gas in it in Alaska, but there is no assurance that something will come out at the other end. You might nationalize something going through your country." There is the nationalization of the potash industry, and stealing cablevision in the area. That is what the latest regulations of the CRTC permit.
For the first time, I found that we were drifting apart ideologically from the United States. They are worried about what is happening in this country and what this government is doing. Mr. Speaker, they have every reason to worry. I did not say that publicly down there, but things were extremely difficult, and they will become more dif-

February 23, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
ficult. Every year we export 80 per cent of our production to the United States, and import between 3 per cent and 5 per cent of their production. If they should close the border to trade tomorrow, we would be eating our pulp, paper and lumber. They can get it from Russia. We have paid for building sawmills in Russia and Poland, and the United States has a trade imbalance because of the wheat that goes over there. We would be eating our pulp and paper tomorrow if the United States were to decide to trade elsewhere. They will eventually have to bring us to reason, and when they do it will hurt us. We will not be number seven in the world, in terms of our standard of living. We will be number twenty-four in other respects and will be treated in the same way as every other banana republic.
Since it was possible at a quarter to twelve, so to speak, to make a back room deal with Reader's Digest, to save face, why is it not possible to make another back room deal with Time and several other companies as well? Surely the minister realizes that the difference between this country and the United States is not great. The Americans respect our wish to evolve our own culture, our wish to build our own nation. They will not sit back forever and take what we have been dishing out to them. They are upset about our foreign take-over legislation and upset about the foreign investment review law. I know we are telling them not to worry, that the decisions so far have been in favour of those who want to invest in Canada. I know that people attending certain United States hearings have told the Americans not to worry, that the law is not being applied strictly, that it is only on the books to keep out certain foreign investment and is seldom, if ever, invoked. The point is that the law is on the statute books and can be invoked.
It is high time this government reaffirmed our country's friendship with the United States. That friendship works in Canada's favour. Continuing on the course this government has set will be devastating for our country. It will alienate us from our friendly, neighbouring giant who may have caused the odd difficulty but who has been a great friend of Canada's ever since we became a nation.
Again I say to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, please call back the people from Time and KVOS and work out another back room deal. After all, pressure is being put on my colleagues from British Columbia. Although they are not as numerous as those who come from Quebec, whose influence was obviously brought to bear with regard to Reader's Digest, I plead with the minister to reconsider the matter, because as many Canadians are employed in Vancouver and British Columbia by companies affiliated with KVOS as are employed in Quebec by Reader's Digest. Obviously, if the minister will not listen, British Columbia members will be disappointed. One hon. member on the government side in particular will be embarrassed when the government's case must again be taken to the people.
I will not prolong this debate because others wish to contribute. It is high time that we, as Canadians, opposed this kind of skullduggery and asked the government to listen to the people, not merely to Tories or Liberals. The minister cannot say that only he on the government side has received letters on this subject. I will not say that I am the only member on my side to whom Canadians write. I

know that the minister and his colleagues are receiving letters of complaint from many Canadians. Before it is too late, I plead with him to reconsider this scandalous course of action and direct this country on a new course.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when last I spoke on this bill in the House I was addressing my remarks to comments made by the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve). We are now discussing an amendment to refer this bill back to commitee. I support the amendment. Having attended committee hearings but, unfortunately, having participated only once in the committee's deliberations, I could not help noting how little time the committee was given to hear the evidence of witnesses. This led to frustration. I am sure that many members and many witnesses were not given the opportunity to voice their concerns in committee about this bill. Let me repeat a comment which the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) made about MD of Canada. She said, as reported on page 10991 of Hansard:
The content of their publication is without fault, I am sure, but this, I must point out, in no way makes it a Canadian magazine.
Magazines like MD of Canada and Modern Medicine, together with agricultural and other professional journals, bring professional and personal enrichment to those who read them. This silly legislation will make such magazines harder to obtain. Some of the present readers may be denied access to them in future. I am sure that the minister and his officials were not thinking of MD of Canada, Modern Medicine, our cattlemen's magazines or other, similar journals when contemplating this law. I doubt if they had ever heard of those magazines. They are not interested in them, and I would not expect the minister to read them; they are outside his interest. But these magazines are part of the lifeblood of professional men, are part of the lifeblood of the various people affected in trades, industries and agriculture. Usually, the reader looks forward to receiving his magazine. Although this law will not make it impossible for people to continue receiving these magazines, it will place constraints on their publication. Perhaps my arguments do not impress the minister; I notice that he yawns. If he had been through the sort of convention I have been through, he might be even more fatigued.
Motion No. 7 was intended to increase television coverage in Canada. The Minister of Communications said that she was concerned about the employment opportunities for Canadian artists and artisans involved with radio and television. She suggested that our artists, artisans and actors did not have adequate opportunities for employment. She went on to suggest that this was an area that required development. She stated it was part of our culture and heritage.
I cannot help but be amazed at the remarks of members opposite when they talk about the need for development of our culture. Last year the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), who is responsible for multiculturalism, was presented with an excellent document, a rather thick manual dealing with the entire subject of multiculturalism. I do not want Your Honour to think I am straying from the purpose and reason for this debate. That manual contained some very valid proposals with regard to multiculturalism. It was

very well done. After all, it was a report commissioned by the government. In July, 1975, I wrote to the Minister of Labour asking about this Canadian cultural identity and the need for a multicultural program. Three weeks later I followed up with another letter because I had not received an acknowledgement. Three weeks later I again followed up with another letter; I had not yet received an acknowledgement.
I followed up the initial letter of July, 1975, with an additional inquiry every three weeks until February, 1976. I have never received the courtesy of a reply. That shows how valid the arguments are by those opposite when they tell us they are concerned about the cultural identity of Canada, how they want to improve our culture and open up opportunities for artists and artisans. If that is an example of what they are doing, then truly it is laughable. I must say, with every measure of scorn, that for a minister to take nine months to answer one simple question is beyond all comprehension. Good heavens, consider what a woman can create in nine months!
The minister has expressed concern about artists and artisans. KVOS made a proposal to the minister which would have given the opportunity to some artists to continue in their present employment. Apparently it was not palatable. Rather than give them that opportunity, the minister would deny them such employment. He would rather they went on UIC and followed through with welfare. That is part of the cultural program of this government. It is a program that is truly remarkable in its lack of identity, thrust and recognition. I do not understand it.
The minister is very concerned about delegating foreign authority to KVOS. She said, in effect, that it is improper for us to accept money from the United States which might in some manner be influential dollars. She said it might improperly influence us, change our culture or change our identity. How naive, at the very least, and how untruthful at the very most. I have never heard any debate in this House about any money put into Canada by a foreigh-con-trolled company such as an oil company or a mining company changing our culture and identity. Surely this is the same thing, but with much smaller dollars. It is better to have something than nothing. Better half a glass of water or half a loaf of bread than nothing at all.
The minister would deny the honest and sincere attempt by KVOS to maintain a presence, a cultural presence at that, in the western part of this country. The minister said, as reported at page 10982 of Hansard:
It is just as if I raised the so-called French problems apropos everything we discussed in the House.
The minister was concerned that we were talking about western alienation. Of course we were talking about western alienation. The minister indicated that this kind of discussion does not take place in the House as far as Quebec is concerned. How very true. It does not need to take place because there are no similar problems in Quebec. We have every assurance that if there were, they would be attended to very quickly. Not so with western Canada. We have every justification in saying there is indeed a problem in western Canada.
Last week the truth of the matter was very evident. We saw the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), his mandarins and ministers, trotting off to British Columbia to solve the
Non-Canadian Publications
problems of the Liberals. What a grand scheme it was. However, I think the appeal of the Prime Minister will have fallen on deaf ears because there are not, and never have been, any tangible results. We see that enormous architectural monstrosity in Vancouver which is called the headquarters of the CBC. I do not doubt that it is very fine on the inside. I wish I could say the same for the outside. When I compare the millions of dollars tied up in that facility to the thousands of dollars that could be spent in my remote constituency in British Columbia, I wonder about the priorities of this government. The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) spoke about the remoteness of his area. I am quite familiar with his part of the country. They do indeed have problems. They are certainly very remote and certainly very northern.
I extend to you, Mr. Speaker, an invitation to come to Kootenay West. You would see that half of our geography stands on its side and a considerable amount is under water. Kootenay West has provided a fortune to the Canadian people. The industriousness of the people has, through Cominco Limited, through mine after mine of silver, lead, zinc, bismuth and antimony provided a fortune in tax revenues of one kind or another. The waterways have provided an enormous source of power-little used in our area, incidentally, because we do not have much industry there; DREE has really not been effective in Kootenay West and has now been withdrawn. Be that as it may, the wealth generated within Kootenay West has contributed a great deal to all of Canada. What has Kootenay West received in return? Consider the communications system. Look at the CBC. We have low-power radio transmitters- LPRTs, as they call them-spotted in three or four areas. In one area the signal goes right by the homes of 350 people, yet they cannot pick it up because the CBC will not spend a dime to enable them to do so; the corporation sends it down the road another 12 miles. How powerful is that mighty signal? Enough to bring it back up the road three miles. How ridiculous!
We are talking about KVOS, about the priorities of the government in the field of communications, whether in print or over the airways. Take the community of Kaslo. They have an LPRT. It has been there several years. The grounding is not very good; people living three miles away cannot pick up the signal. Do we find the CBC very concerned about this? The minister has talked about the legality of these things. We heard the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River tell us about people in his communities having provided their own signals. I suspect it is almost too much to accept as mere coincidence the fact that the CRTC hearings involving the CBC took place at almost the same time as the debate on Bill C-58 began in this House. It was interesting to hear the Minister of Communications talking about legality, telling us this was illegal and that was illegal. Yet I have not heard one word from the hon. lady with reference to the fact that the tower which was erected on Mount Seymour was erected in violation of CRTC regulations. I addressed the hearing in Vancouver and pointed this out, but I have yet to hear a response. I can only assume the CBC will continue to break not only the regulations of the CRTC, with the full

February 23, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
approval of that body, but also the provisions of the Criminal Code.
If the minister cares to read my presentation before the CRTC, he will find out that the CBC is violating the law time after time. How laughable it is! The CRTC and the CBC are in bed together, yet the CRTC tells my people that they cannot put in a transmitter or that they cannot put in a receiver. Talk about mixed priorities! The Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) is very concerned about KVOS. I trust she is not laughing over the fact the CRTC condones the violation of regulations by the CBC. I am glad the hon. lady, by shaking her head, gives me reassurance on that point. Right now, CTV is going into Kootenay West having been asked to do so by the residents. After the CRTC changed the ground rules a bit, delaying the plan for a year and frustrating the people in my riding still further, the green light has finally been given, as I understand it.
I know the system being used by CTV is a very costly one and I know, also, it is not likely to show much of a profit for CTV. That is one of the penalties of doing business. Were it not for channels 2, 4 and 6, and channel 7 out of Spokane, the residents of Kootenay West would not have had an opportunity to watch television at all. These stations were there years before CBC ever got off its backside and provided a signal.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the communications history of my riding, and the picture is not much different throughout the outlying areas of British Columbia. At this very moment the people north of latitude 60 have a better communications link than the people of Kootenay West. Surely there has to be something wrong with the government's priorities when it comes to the operation of its communications network.

speechtext: The minister is leaving.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
How unfortunate. Here I was, making such a sterling address, and the minister has abandoned me. I feel crushed. In any event, back on February 10 the Minister of Communications, as reported at page 10,823 of Hansard, said she was concerned about special tax deals. How, she asked, could a government make some kind of special arrangement with KVOS? That is an intriguing question, and I hope the minister was directing it to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) rather than to us, because the Minister of Finance is an expert at making special appeals when it comes to taxation.
There is nothing original or strange about making some kind of tax arrangement with a foreign firm, whether it is a television company, a mining company or an oil company, whether it is located in the United States, in Cuba or in some other country. I am sure the government has sufficient experience to develop any special arrangements which may be desired. Certainly when it comes to taxation, the Minister of Finance and his colleagues have demonstrated a supreme capacity for making special deals. I see no reason why there should be any difficulty at all in dealing with the tax position as it affects KVOS. KVOS has dealt very well with Canadians when it comes to taxation, just as they have with their own country; that is to say, on the basis of a 50-50 sharing arrangement. Perhaps the ministry in Canada would like more.

In urging hon. members to return this bill to committee, I say this: it is obvious to all Canadians, and particularly to all members of the House, that the debate on Bill C-58 has been prolonged for more than the normal period. Why has debate on this bill, at every stage and on every motion, been so protracted? The answer is, because there is so much which is wrong with this legislation, wrong with the whole thrust and purpose of the measure. Obviously, the government is prepared to wait it out. Let me assure the government that it is not our intention to test its patience; but we, too, are very patient and intend to examine thoroughly, at every opportunity, every facet of the bill that is wrong, as well as those amendments that were defeated by members on the other side.
I wonder how those in the healing profession on the other side of the House, who have so quickly, in such a trained seal fashion, jumped up to support their government, will relate their position when it comes to such professional journals as MD of Canada and Modern Medicine, as well as certain trade and agricultural journals. It may well be that the professionals on the other side of the House are really not interested in these kinds of magazines and they could care less. They are not concerned whether their fellow doctors or fellow farmers or lawyers have the opportunity to enrich themselves with any opportunity for culture or professional development.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: They want to be brainwashed.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
It may well be that they have some difficulty reading. In the context of this bill it has been said that there may be some form of United States retaliation. This proposition has been rejected by the government, and rightly so. I, too, would reject it. The United States really does not play that kind of game. If it does, it does it in a very sloppy fashion. In talking on this bill, it is our purpose, at least in part, to see that Canada does not have the opportunity to play that kind of game, the retaliation game engineered by members on the other side of the House. I do not suppose for a moment that the United States would take some arbitrary form of retaliation. I am sure none of us is worried about a nuclear strike.
Nevertheless, I suggest the opportunity is there for the United States to say, "Well, we had better keep our signals within the United States. Canadians are not interested in them; they do not want them, or at least the government does not". It is not very difficult, technically speaking, to keep U.S. signals in the United States, though I hope that does not happen. But if it does happen, I suggest there would probably be a subsequent strike within the postal service because it could not handle the volume of mail that the Minister of Communications, the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner), the Prime Minister, and all members on that side of the House would receive as a result.
The minister is more concerned about our cultural identity than she is about freedom of the press and the airwaves. Regardless of all the rhetoric and speeches that have been made, the simple fact remains, so far as KVOS are concerned, that they are quite prepared to act within the rules. They are quite prepared to accept the same
February 23, 1976

treatment that Canadian stations receive when their signals go across the border.
One critic corralled me outside the House and said, "You are wrong. How can you make statements such as you have just made if that station is not prepared to entertain 80 per cent Canadian ownership?" At least, I think that was the percentage he threw at me. I ask, Mr. Speaker, why should they? Does the United States insist upon 80 per cent ownership of signals originating in Canada? I would be very pleased to hear of just one case. Surely there are some experts on the other side who can advise me whether the United States insists upon 80 per cent U.S. ownership of Canadian signals going into the United States. What utter nonsense!
Let us send this bill back to the committee where it belongs. Let us have a full review by the Secretary of State, the Minister of Communications and all the other experts on that side who have managed to cloud, garble and distort the bill with non-persuasive arguments. Let us then get on with other business in this House. Another most controversial bill introduced by this government, Bill C-68-another cop-out by the federal government-is awaiting us in the wings and requires the attention of the members of the House. There are, of course, other bills waiting, bills requiring the attention of the House. We can only assume that in his wisdom the House leader has decided that debate on Bill C-58 must continue ad nauseam and ad infinitum. If that be the case, the policy of those on this side of the House who are concerning themselves with this particular bill will be "illegitimi non carborundum."
