subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member has some constructive comments to make, though I think he ought to recognize that he is dealing with a minister who has put forward a pretty sloppy bill, one that had loopholes which had to be patched up as we went along, a sloppy enough bill that special concessions have now been made to certain groups which the bill originally attacked. I suggest this is all very much in character with the role that the minister himself has played in committee and in the House. He is a minister who, basically, is not in his seat for the question period. He is not in his seat now, during the debate on this bill. I cannot for the life of me believe that a person who would put forward a bill of such interest to the Canadian public would not remain to hear it debated.
I know of no bill that has attracted as much mail sent to members of the House as this bill, yet the minister and other members of the Privy Council are not even in their seats. I think this is a real slam to the Canadian public that their democratic process is being so totally denied. It has been said that the purpose of this bill is to protect our cultural identity. That identity cannot be protected by such a flippant attitude on the part of hon. members opposite.
The purpose of this amendment is simply to send the bill back to the committee. I suggest it ought to go back to the committee because it is legislation which has been etched in the minds of the Canadian public as a disservice. It has caused discontent across this country and has resulted in great protests coming to the desks of members of parliament. We have received literally thousands of letters of protest. My filing cabinet has letters of protest from constituents measuring eight to ten inches thick.
All that is being asked is that the bill be sent back to the committee in order that we can rehear the witnesses under new circumstances which result from the fact that the government has chosen to change the legislation. It originally put forward a legislative measure which would deny

Non-Canadian Publications
Reader's Digest certain tax benefits. The government then changed its mind and said Reader's Digest would qualify, but continued to deny the benefits to other publications. What must be clarified and made crystal clear are the rules of this game. How can any publishing group in this country, Canadian or otherwise, have any sense of security about the publishing industry here when we have a government that changes the rules according to its own whims, choosing its own friends and enemies. That is exactly what has happened.
The claim by some, that this is a Maclean-Hunter bill, has some validity. One only has to look at Maclean's magazine since it changed from a publication every two weeks. It is now, obviously, a Liberal magazine. One only has to count the number of Liberal cabinet ministers who have been on the cover picture of this magazine. The fact of the matter is that this is a bill designed to kill the counterparts of Maclean's, for the protection of the government's own supporters. If that is not the case, then how can one justify the treatment given Reader's Digest and the treatment extended to Time magazine?
The issue here is clear. The reason for sending this piece of legislation back to the committee is to define the criteria-criteria that have become very clouded and, I suggest, very shady. This is a very unscrupulous issue that faces us because of the lack of definition of criteria and lack of clarity in direction. We are now asking the government for a chance to find out, once and for all, what the government is trying to do. It is almost impossible to debate this piece of legislation in this House because it is so pointless and without direction.
By putting forward a piece of legislation without spelling out the criteria in respect of allowing foreign publications into this country, the government forces a subjective judgment, and as long as the judgment is subjective, regardless of what other government considerations may be advanced in support of the bill, the fact is the legislation is a form of censorship. For this reason, we ask that the bill be returned to the committee. Perhaps, more properly, we ought to suggest it be returned to the wastepaper basket. The bill ought not to be before us because of the obvious loopholes, to say nothing of the basic and clear lack of philosophy behind it.
We are asking the government, during this debate, to make it very clear how a publication is to be considered Canadian. We also want to know who is to make the decision. How can any company publishing material for the market in Canada develop a set of criteria when it does not know what the government has in mind? We have had no clear answer in this House whether MD of Canada will fit into the mainstream of Canadian publications. Nor do we know what MD of Canada requires to do in order to fit into this mainstream.
MD of Canada collects its medical information from all around the world, so obviously most of its material is foreign. Is the research in different nations of the world not of value in Canada? Is science and scientific research in any part of the world valid in this country? Is not the fact that MD of Canada is essentially a Canadian-owned magazine, using foreign material, a valid reason for publication in this country?

The question at issue here relates to the exemption of Reader's Digest and how it, in fact, meets the criteria, however unclear they may be. Apparently the decision in respect of all magazines is to be left in the hands of the government in order that it can tinker with and shape the minds of the Canadian people. The decisions are to be made at the government's whim. I suggest that if the government has no business in the bedrooms of the nation, is has no business in the minds of the citizens.
We can say with certainty that one of the reasons for this bill is to provide the government with the means of shaping Canadian thought, and shaping it deliberately according to the wish and the will of the government. This is a deliberate and unscrupulous attempt at censorship. It is designed to put forward specific ideas of the government to the Canadian people and to provide patronage to certain areas. It is designed to find favour in respect of certain magazines and to provide employment in specific areas. How else can the government justify its special exemption for Reader's Digest, a privilege that has been withheld from other magazines?
We must have a clear definition of criteria in order that magazines published outside the borders of this country will have some clear direction of what needs to be done to get into the Canadian market. We need some clear rationale in order that people will feel a sense of security in the publishing industry. We must know why some magazines are being denied the privilege of publishing here without having to pay a surtax.
Let us look at the principle of censorship itself. We know that at times there have been valid reasons for censorship in this country, yet the government has denied that censorship. I recall different ministers saying they did not believe in censorship. The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) made this clear in committee. I do not, personally, believe in censorship and I think censorship ought not to be the role of government. Does it not strike you as odd, Mr. Speaker, that thousands and thousands of letters have crossed the desks of members of parliament in protest against certain CBC programs, namely, "Ten Lost Years", "Baptism", and "You Are Going To Be All Right, Jamie Boy", yet the government simply passed these off by saying it would not enter into any form of censorship? On the other hand, we have the present situation. The government has imposed its own will in respect of a change in rules as they apply to a certain publication.
On one hand there is the right to avoid the use of material that might be offensive to some, or reverse the government's choice to ban it, as in the case of Reader's Digest, MD of Canada, Time magazine and, I suppose, even the Bible inasmuch as its content is at least 80 per cent foreign. We certainly must ask what the government uses as its criteria. Partly tongue in cheek, and partly seriously, I suggest that the government might consider the Bible to have foreign content. I notice members opposite smiling. The fact is that if they wanted to be literal in respect of their own legislation, they could put a degree of control on anything they wanted at the whim and will of the government.
February 23, 1976

I think this brings us to the basic question of the Bill of Rights in this country and the privilege of being Canadian. As I understand the Bill of Rights, it ought not to have a price, a tax or a surtax attached to it. To this government, the right to information means that if the people want certain bits of information they can get it, but at a price.
I should like to know from members on the government side whether this is a philosophy that will apply to all rights in this country, and at whose wish and whim, and at what point, will the criteria be established and set out in legislation so that we will know what allows Reader's Digest in and what keeps Time magazine out, because without that defined criteria there is no doubt that this is a censorship bill. To claim otherwise is to be stupid, because the fact is that no one has yet explained to this House precisely why Reader's Digest was able to obtain a special exemption, and whether or not other companies which have not obtained the exemption can do something in order to meet the qualifications. Is that not a silly way to run a government? Is that not an unfortunate way to operate an institution which exists within a democracy?
The government sets up something which is so loose as to be totally subject to its will. This must be treated as a threat to all Canadians, because although it applies to some little piece of paper such as Bill C-58, which means that we may not get Reader's Digest next month, it is also an indication that this government has chosen to interfere with the basic rights of Canadians because it chooses to stop something without establishing criteria in respect of what might be stopped.
The government makes special exemptions in order to get around the stop-measures without establishing the criteria in this regard. What this boils down to is simply that the government has opted to set up for itself a subjective position in which it says it has the privilege and right to influence the public mind for its purpose. That is a most unfortunate situation. We can claim that the bill does not have a political mandate, and well it does not. Did anyone hear, during any election called by the Liberals in recent times, that one of their intentions was to impose upon Canadians a restriction on certain publications? They know they have been dishonest in their electioneering. They did not put forward any particular set of examples to illustrate to the Canadian people that this was expected. Yet this has been imposed. I think this points out the philosophy of the government of the day. It has the notion it has the right to do whatever it wants. Once they have won, they get the feeling that they might not win again unless somehow they can shape the minds of Canadians.
One way to do this is to try to restrict the information available to Canadians. They do not want to call it a censorship bill because that might bring a strong reaction, so they slip it in bit by bit in an effort to control the minds of Canadians. The bill has as its single purpose an attempt to control the minds of Canadians under the guise of an attempt to protect some irregularities in the taxing system. If that was all the government wanted to do, this bill would have gone through much sooner. I do not think there would have been much objection from this side if that had been the sole purpose.
When members of the government claim that the opposition is holding up this bill, they are simply blowing and
Non-Canadian Publications
sucking at the same time while trying to maintain a whirlwind attack. In this country the people have a right to think. They have a right to think, to read, to hear, to speak and to communicate as a principle of the Bills of Rights. This government is imposing its view in respect of the information available to the Canadian people. I have claimed before that this is a censorship bill because it sets out, in almost its only set of criteria about publications, a set of criteria that is false.
They talk about how foreign publications must be at least 80 per cent different in content to any previous publication. A simple analysis of that boils down to the fact that there is no such thing as 80 per cent. It does not exist. It cannot apply to publications. This government knows that. Percent is a mathematical concept. It is used in mathematical terms. You can talk about mathematical notions and percentages when talking about such units of measurement as length, weight or volume; you can talk about a percentage increase or decrease in the use of numbers. But you cannot talk about percent in dealing with values. That is like saying to someone that a person is 80 per cent right or, "I hate you 80 per cent", or that someone loves someone else 63 per cent.
The government takes a piece of legislation and tries to relate 80 per cent to a value judgment. This is a false concept. Someone can take a look at something, and if they do not like it they can say it is not 80 per cent. If they do not like it they can claim it is any per cent, because there is no unit of measurement for a value judgment. It is only when there are units of measurement that a percentage may be taken. It is a phony government that tries to tell us this criteria of 80 per cent has any validity. Anyone who has taken a course in research knows there is no way one can look at a piece of literature and apply 80 per cent to it with any degree of consistency.
This issue came up during the committee hearings on this legislation. I challenged the deputy minister, who was on hand that day and who had said they would use the length as the unit of measure; I asked him, if we had a piece of information that was 100 centimetres long and boiled it down until it was only 20 centimetres long, but had basically the same concept, whether that would apply. He said yes, to which the minister piped up and said it would not, that it must differ substantially, meaning that it must be different in its content or in what it talks about. This means the government is saying it is putting on a subjective judgment, that the percent notion no longer applies and that this government is censoring the minds of Canadians.
There is no doubt that, and I think it is time the government recognized that they are putting forward a piece of legislation which threatens the very core of what this country is intended to stand for. All the while the debate goes on, and the minister slips in and out of the House without showing sufficient interest to take part in the debate while hon. members have been speaking this afternoon. It is most unfortunate that such an attitude should prevail on the other side, because if we are going to look at a bill which has as one of its objectives the influencing of Canadian culture, the least we could ask is that the debate be approached with a less flippant attitude.

Non-Canadian Publications
We know that the government accepts certain magazines and rejects others, without establishing any criteria, that it talks about 80 per cent when percentage should not apply, and that it censors the minds of Canadians. In fact, it tries to shape this country in such a way that the publishing industry is led to failure. The government would like to support Maclean-Hunter so its members can have their pictures week after week on its front page. It does all that, simply to try to maintain power. The whole bill is aimed at nothing else than destroying the whole notion of parliamentary democracy.
How can the government be bothered with this piece of legislation when there are so many inequities in the communications field with which they could be dealing? If the minister is really sincere about doing something for Canadians, how is it that the citizens in east central Alberta and west central Saskatchewan, who cannot pick up the CBC radio signal at night, receive a reply to their complaint from the Secretary of State, only a week ago, in a letter which stated that the CBC tests the strength of the signal in daytime, and if the people cannot get a night signal that is unfortunate? How is it that the television reception in the same communities is totally inadequate, yet the response of the government has been that perhaps by 1978 there will be some opportunities to put up another satellite transmitter?
Why is it that this bill is before us and takes up the time of the House, when people in the Northwest Territories, such as in Yellowknife, have to receive their news between midnight and one o'clock in the morning? I suppose the only justification for that is that when the Liberal government is in power the news is so bad that the government must set up a protective policy for the people in the north. Why is it that people in Yellowknife, when the weather is 40 below, have to listen to weather reports stating that it is raining outside, because the signal comes from Vancouver? Why is it that people whose natural trading links are with the northern cities of Edmonton and Saskatoon are unnaturally linked with Vancouver? This is a bill which should not be before members of parliament because the citizens of this country are asking for consideration of other issues in the field of communications. This is a bill which imposes on people, not responds to the needs and wishes of the citizens of this country.
Let us take a look at another portion of this senseless bill, a bill which indiscriminately opposes borderline broadcasting whereby U.S. stations beam their signals in Canada. I accept that there could be some real and genuine concern if all our culture were to come from the south across the forty-ninth parallel. But rather than react in the way in which the government has reacted in such an uptight manner about Americans influencing our culture, why do they not recognize that in the age in which we live, in the 1970s and the 1980s, and in the compressed world in which we can communicate instantaneously with any continent, instead of restricting any communication across the border we should open it up, and instead of requesting borderline conferences on communications between our two countries we should request the U.S. to encourage considerably more Canadian programs in that country?
One of the objectives of this bill was to increase opportunities for Canadian cultural development. How can it be

done better than by opening up the market to Canadians? However, that is not possible for a restrictive government which wants to control. This government does not care about the expansion of cultural concepts, but would rather control broadcasting. If it really cared to expand our cultural influence, it would open the market wider and it would not have taken such a hard position on KVOS, one of the best examples of good Canadian corporate citizenship. KVOS, over 20 years ago, on its own initiative approached the Canadian government and asked to pay Canadian income tax because it recognized that a significant number of its dollars came from Canada. Some of the money from this company started Canawest, which now employs hundreds of people in the animated film industry in the production of animated advertisements not only used in Canada but used in the television market throughout North America and the world.
This piece of legislation, insensitive as it is, takes the position, on the one hand, that we should try to expand Canadian culture, and on the other scrambles the eggs by beating the chicken. There is no sense or logic in the legislation before us, and I submit the least that members of the government could do would be to send this bill back to the committee for the purpose of hearing more witnesses and to try to crystallize and clarify what is now a totally hazy, foggy and subjective approach to legislation the aim of which seems to be censorship.
To suggest that this legislation can be given third reading is to be naive beyond belief. It has not been prepared in any kind of finite detail. The government cannot tell us honestly in the House the ramifications of this bill with regard to any foreign publication, because it has not established the criteria. It does not know what will happen to a company which is foreign owned if it sells its shares to a Canadian operation, because it has not established its criteria. All we can say is that because the government cannot accept the challenge to send this bill back to the committee, it is chicken and it does not want to hear the Canadian people give testimony and bear witness in a way in which might be embarrassing to the government. The government could well improve its position if it could swallow hard and realize that this bill is as flippant as the minister himself. It should recognize that it would be much better to withdraw it or, failing that, send it back to committee to be tightened up.
Members of the government have become turncoat on Reader's Digest without telling us why but they are still hard-liners on Time, and without telling us how. They are a subjective government making decisions which affect the lives of Canadians, without reason, without criteria, without concern. Their position on this legislation is symbolic of a much greater issue, one which relates to the Bill of Rights and the concepts and freedoms we find therein. This legislation in its present form would put a price tag on certain freedoms which would then fall into the domain of privilege, with the government having the power to extend or restrict them at will. What folly for any government to take that position.
The plea of this party is that the government extend the time for consideration of this bill in committee so that an attempt can be made to iron out the problems that remain
February 23, 1976

and so that we can understand more fully the intention of the legislation.
I consider it a threat that the government would take the position that it should control the flow of knowledge and has the right to shape the minds of Canadian citizens. It is playing foul with the heritage of this country without reason, without concern, and certainly without the consent of the citizens, and I think it is high time that members of the government answered for that.
Three times in committee and in this House, Mr. Speaker, I have issued the challenge for anyone on the government side to explain what unit of measurement will determine the 80 per cent rule, but have never had a response. The plain fact is that there is no such thing as a percentage in a value judgment. If something cannot be measured by weight, volume or length, as greater or smaller numerically, there is no such thing as a percentage. The government knows it is playing with a false notion.
The government is making a deliberate attempt to mislead the Canadian people by saying, "We will allow at least 20 per cent foreign material into the country". The truth of the matter is that percentages do not apply. The government is playing censor and ought to be called for that, and called because it is being dishonest about the intent of the legislation. I think it has been deliberately dishonest, Mr. Speaker-dishonest about the fact that it hoped this legislation could be used as a tool or a ploy; it is a malicious attempt by the government to shape the minds of Canadians to its own advantage.
I issue the challenge to any member of the government who wants to respond in this debate to rise and tell us the unit of measurement of the value judgment that applies. How is it measured? How do you look at a painting and say it is 80 per cent pretty? How do you look at literature and say it is 80 per cent different? It cannot be done. The government's position is false and it really threatens the whole parliamentary system if it thinks this kind of unscrupulous and untidy legislation can pass.
The Liberal government is trying to sneak this bill in through the back door without considering the wishes of Canadian people. Across the nation many Canadians are voicing their concern about the communications system, their concern about violent and abusive material on television and in the media, while the government chooses to censor Reader's Digest, Time and MD of Canada without giving reason. Then the next news was that Reader's Digest was acceptable.
I note that the minister has returned to the House from his vacation in his office. I wonder if at this time we might adjourn my speech and suggest to him-oh, I see he has left again. I suppose he thought I was going to make a suggestion to him and did not stay around for it. I would suggest that the minister rise in this House and tell us how it is possible to apply percentages to a value judgment. I do not believe the minister can honestly tell us that the 80 per cent criteria is even slightly honest. He knows a bureaucracy has been set up to attribute to a piece of literature any percentage it likes-according to how it likes the literature. There is no way to attach a mathematical concept to a value judgment. If the minister cannot define it for us he should face the fact that the government is submitting a
Non-Canadian Publications
censorship bill and attempting to play with the minds of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, this is the third or fourth time I have spoken at various stages of this particular legislation. This is a bad bill. The objectives and intentions of the minister that led to the legislation were good objectives and good intentions, and I say that without reservation. But it is bad legislation.
Given the good intentions and good objectives I suggest that the legislation was conceived in ignorance, drafted in a world of fantasy and, if passed, will be implemented in chaos. I do not know the way out.

speechtext:
The motion put forward by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) suggests that the matter be referred back to committee. I support the motion, for a number of reasons. First, I have faith, possibly a naive faith, in that particular committee. I served on it for more than three years, did battle in it with esteemed friends opposite, enjoyed my battles, and enjoyed the results of some of those battles.
In the last parliament the committee considered broadcasts in Gaelic for Cape Breton. I remember the consideration regarding the export of Canadian cultural property. I remember complimenting the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) on third reading. Yes, we have had harsh words in that committee, but we have always served under a fair and just chairman. His successor, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), was no less an honourable chairman. Therefore I support this motion because these difficulties cannot be resolved in the House and there is some hope, albeit remote, of resolving them in committee.
I regret the atmosphere of the committee hearings. I am not debating who ought to have been on it and who ought not, who said what and why, and who could sit on it and who could not. I also regret the lack of time the committee was given to examine witnesses whose expert evidence was worth hearing. I found an atmosphere of acrimony. I did not see the adversary system working. I believe in the adversary system. No, I found "chippiness," a lack of flexibility and a lack of respect for opposite viewpoints. This I had never seen in that committee. I do not think this legislation will destroy the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, but I do know that what we do with this bill may affect other legislation coming before the committee. This is not easy legislation; the citizenship bill will not be easy legislation either. I know I am straying, Mr. Speaker, and I appreciate your indulgence.
It is my opinion that the only hope for this bad bill lies in that committee. I want to see the integrity of the committee restored because, in my judgment, what it did with Bill C-58 eroded its integrity. In saying this I do not point my finger at the minister, whip, or government supporters on the committee.

February 23, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
I am happy to see my good friend, the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Douglas) in the House. He spoke on a motion dealing with the broadcasting part of the bill, and made a good speech. We gave him a rough time when he spoke. I compliment him for speaking. At least I know how he feels. I do not know what the Secretary of State and Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) feel because the government's position has changed radically since the introduction of this legislation. At least I know where my colleague from Bruce-Grey stands, even though I know he is wrong.
Second, I think the committee could resolve the uncertainty surrounding this legislation ever since January 1975. Difficult legislation like this inevitably leads to uncertainty. I find some aspects of the bill completely acceptable. I favour a healthy magazine industry in Canada. I accept that we must protect that industry from unfair competition. I accept the ownership provisions of the bill, although I do not know if there is any magic in 75 per cent. I enthusiastically support provisions concerning editing and publishing in Canada. Frankly, they do not go far enough. The minister might have gone further to Canadianize the publishing industry. Why are there no provisions concerning circulation, advertising, personnel, accounting, and so on, provisions which could Canadianize to a greater extent the publishing industry? I will not make an issue of this.
Let me tell the minister what I cannot accept. I am against two aspects of the bill. I oppose the government's content approach. I would be willing to consider an antidumping approach. I do not know how difficult this would be. I am sure the minister and his officials are much more expert in this field than I am, and perhaps they have considered the anti-dumping approach. Let me make my position clear: I prefer the anti-dumping approach, by way of legislation, to the content route. However, I suppose it is too late in the day for this. As I say, I wish the minister and his officials had taken that route, instead of the "substantially the same" route. Actually nothing I have heard in this House or elsewhere suggests that the government has even considered this approach.
The second aspect I cannot accept is the aspect of back room deals. Mr. Speaker, back room deals are destroying the integrity of the Department of National Revenue, destroying the integrity of a department whose integrity must never be in doubt.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I cannot accept the wheeling and dealing. If the wheeling and dealing were laid on the table, were opened up for all to see, there might be justification for it. We do not know the government's reasons for wanting to get rid of Time but to keep Reader's Digest. I do not accept that process. It is not an honourablte process to which this House should be party. Possibly the committee might resolve these two difficulties. I do not know, but I think the minister ought to be fair and try it.
Several other areas of the bill concern me. The minister indicated he might look at the distribution system. I understand that 13 of 14 magazine distribution companies working in this country are U.S.-controlled. I know I may be out of order, Mr. Speaker, but the system of distribution of periodicals concerns me very much.

The minister may be fed up to the ears with hearing about Time, but one point merits repeating. Time was misled. I do not say it was deliberate. When the magazine presented its first mock-up to officials of the Department of National Revenue it understood that Canadian content meant roughly 42 per cent of content. The officials in good faith were thinking in terms of 50 per cent or 60 per cent. Why did Time return shortly afterwards with a revised mock-up? I do not understand why the department did not respond to that mock-up, unless somewhere along the line somebody pulled a switch or pushed a button and said, "Stop; we cannot win what we want with this mock-up." If you are going to be cynical you could say the button was pushed because Maclean-Hunter said they needed 80 per cent. I am not going to be that cynical, but it is a conclusion one could draw.
There is no doubt that something happened at some stage, probably on May 5 or 6, 1975, to cause the officials in the Department of National Revenue to say stay away from the Time mock-up deal because we are not on that any more. Something happened in October and, all of a sudden, it became 80 per cent. Again if one were cynical one could say that Maclean-Hunter really wanted 100 per cent, but they could get away with 80 per cent. I am not saying that because I am not cynical.
The other magazine that really concerns me is MD of Canada. I do not understand why it is being executed. One member opposite, I believe the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy), proposed an amendment to solve that problem. I forget the exact words, but it included all scientific publications. I supported that amendment.
I cannot understand the objects. First there is the antidumping object and, second, the encouragement of the Canadian industry. Why are we on a witch-hunt against MD and similar publications? If Reader's Digest can be accommodated through a back room deal, why can MD not get into the same room? There are other publications in the same general category as MD of Canada. I do not know if it is a locked door into that room. If so, it is very unfortunate because that is not the experience I have had with the Department of National Revenue over the years.
I usually hear cries of "obstruction" and "filibuster". I thank members opposite for not saying that today. However, I was prepared to accept it as being reasonably accurate. In January, 1975, there was the removal of what is called the grandfather clause subsequent to which there was no consultation of any significant nature with those against whom the legislation was drafted to operate. There was no reasonable consultation basically with Time and Reader's Digest.
This is tax legislation. Therefore it is penal legislation. A lack of consultation with those being penalized gives little credit to those in government responsible for the legislation. Therefore I do not mind speaking on this at length. I do not mind if many of my colleagues in this party join me in this. If that is obstruction we should not be reluctant to accept the label.
In May, 1975, Time was misled by the then Minister of National Revenue with regard to this mock-up. If that were to happen again it would encourage me to obstruct
February 23, 1976

again or filibuster.If that is the label, I accept it. If someone had been considered Canadian under our laws for a substantial length of time and was misled by an arm of this government, namely the Department of National Revenue, I see no reason why those in opposition and, frankly, those on the government benches should not obstruct or filibuster.
In October, 1975, we were confronted with the so-called Cullen rule, the result of which was to change the content percentage. The second result was to give publishers ten weeks to conform. I do not mind obstructing that kind of legislation or rule. If that is filibustering or obstruction, I will accept the label. When I saw the atmosphere in the standing committee and what was done to make that committee less effective than it had been historically, I saw good reason to stand up and obstruct. I do not consider that obstruction negative. I consider it positive.
The only hope for this legislation is to let it go back to committee. I am almost sympathetic with the fact that the government has a political football and it does not know whether to kick, pass or run. Therefore it is fumbling. It has pretty well consistently fumbled from January, 1975, to February 23, 1976.
I again say that this is bad legislation, conceived in ignorance, drafted in a world of fantasy and, if implemented, will result in chaos. I urge this House to accept the motion of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock. In my judgment the only hope for this legislation, if there is any hope at all, lies in the standing committee.

The difficulty about the bill before us is that its provisions, coupled with the rules which have been promulgated by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen), imply a new departure in the field of legislation. I know of no other instance in which a bill, in relation to its most important principles, leans for support on something which is outside the bill, namely, something which can be changed, interpreted or adjusted according to the outlook of a particular minister or a particular government. This is why the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) moved that the bill be referred back to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts to enable that committee to hear evidence concerning the arrangements made after Bill C-58 had been reported to the House, the arrangements being those which would enable Reader's Digest to qualify as a Canadian periodical.
The extent of this arrangement is an important thing for the Canadian people to know. One legislative sin has already been committeed, and that is the acceptance of the so-called Cullen rule. The second sin is the government's failure to come clean with the House, as it were, about the line it is taking in this respect; as matters stand I really do not know how the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) feels about this. He has been silent. A very important part of the package is not included in the legislation and is subject to change without ever coming before the House.
Speaking just before the dinner adjournment, the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) indicated on behalf of this party that we find the "content" approach taken on the part of the government, albeit toward a worthy object, unacceptable to us. We would like the minister, instead, to consider, adopting an anti-dumping approach. We cannot accept any arrangement which even appears to have a tinge of a back room deal about it. Even the appearance of such an arrangement lends some credence to a charge of this kind when that charge is not denied.
We are concerned as well about whether or not the particular attitude evinced by the Cullen rule accompanying this piece of legislation could be extended by a government to other forms of periodicals and reading material such as newspapers. I think it is important to remember that as this debate began the newspaper editorial writers and commentators indicated that the word censorship used in terms of this legislation was too strong. Then as the case unfolded the attitude of these same newspaper columnists and commentators changed, to the point where now they are almost universally opposed to a system of justice

The government ought to disclose to the House the background to the arrangement, and who made it. The reasons for the arrangement ought to be explored in depth by a committee, and witnesses should be called so they can be questioned by members of the committee. A complete parliamentary re-examination of the bill should take place. subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would strongly support sending this bill back to committee so that the so-called Cullen rule, which appears to be nothing more than a rule designed in the head of the minister of the day, or of some civil servant to fit the needs of any given situation, can be examined. As a result of this sweetheart deal with Reader's Digest which has gained it Canadian status, everything becomes very murky and the thing smells of political patronage. Obviously Reader's Digest was desired by a large number of Canadians, but more important its offices were situated in the city of Montreal. Time is entitled to ask why its position should not be re-axamined in light of this so-called Cullen rule. In fact the whole magazine industry may well be placed back in the situation it was before.
In effect the government has nullified about 25 per cent of what it hoped to save on advertising-some $10 million in Time and some $7 million in Reader's Digest, the balance being in the broadcasting media. For more than a decade Canadian companies advertising in foreign owned publications aimed primarily at the Canadian market have not been permitted to deduct advertising costs. This shows a great deal of decision by the revenue department. Just the other day I noticed an advertisement by CP Air in Newsweek designed for the Canadian market, since it showed only airline routes in Canada. The new rule applies to editorial content that is not substantially the same as the content of a foreign publication with which there is a continuing relationship. It is this "continuing relationship" that I think needs examination.
I think the government hopes to save about $40 million, though this has been cut to $30 million. There is no reason for assuming that the government ever will save $40 million, but let us examine what has happened under this sweetheart deal and the application of the Cullen rule. Although the terms of the bill are the same as originally, the government is putting a different interpretation upon it.
(Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton).]
Last October the revenue minister decreed that "not substantially the same as" meant "80 per cent different". Since neither magazine felt it could meet this difference, they had to cease publication. The government has now come up with a different interpretation. The phrase "not substantially the same as" remains unchanged; it is still 80 per cent different. The new interpretation relates to what constitutes a "continuing relationship". The aim of the bill is now entirely different.
The revenue minister has suggested that Reader's Digest can still operate in Canada if its editorials fall into any of three categories. The first is that of original articles written for Reader's Digest of Canada. That is fairly easy to achieve; all that has to be done is to publish an article in Canada first and then send it to the United States for publication. It is really a negation of the whole concept of what is an original article for Reader's Digest of Canada.
The second category concerns articles that have appeared in other publications with which Reader's Digest of Canada has no continuing relationship. Obviously this could relate to any of the sub-companies owned by Reader's Digest.
The third category is articles purchased through Reader's Digest of the United States which have been chosen, edited, and condensed by Reader's Digest of Canada. Again these articles must be chosen from publications with which Reader's Digest of Canada has no continuing relationship. It is this third category that is the crucial one.
In effect, Madam Speaker, the government is saying that Reader's Digest of Canada has no continuing relationship with Reader's Digest of the United States if Reader's Digest of Canada merely buys articles through Reader's Digest of the United States; in other words, if it buys articles that appeared elsewhere, using Reader's Digest of the United States as an intermediary. The whole situation is so complicated that it can be interpreted in any way the revenue department wants.
As a result of this interpretation of what is a continuing relationship, Reader's Digest of Canada is completely whitewashed. It is now in the category of being 80 per cent different. Time of Canada cannot buy articles through Time of the United States because the Time organization originates its own material. Therefore Time Canada can buy only from Time of the United States and thus is considered to have a continuing relationship. Obviously it was a sharp eyed person in the department who spotted that and used it to fabricate a rule to keep out Time but allow Reader's Digest of Canada to continue. This House should have a look at this problem to find out why one is allowed in and the other is not. It is obvious that Time will not be allowed because it represents competition to the hopefully to be published Maclean-Hunter weekly.
Let me say a few words about two or three medical journals that will be affected by this legislation, and I have specifically in mind MD Canada, Modern Medicine and The Medical Aspects of Human Sexuality. These are small but very well published magazines. MD Canada is a standout because it portrays the history of medicine. The articles are well written, much like those that appear in the heritage works of the Horizon magazine from New York, which
February 23, 1976

is probably the most outstanding in the world. It seems foolish to get rid of these magazines.
The opportunity to publish the results of Canadian research is very thin at the best of times. Much of the work the National Research Council does in respect of medical matters is lost because there is no way of publishing it. When a researcher is finished he sends his material to the archives here in Ottawa where it sits on a shelf gathering dust. No one ever sees that work again. Very soon the Research Council forgets about it and appropriates another $50,000 or so to research the very thing that was done in the first place.
The Canadian Medical Journal is the only medical magazine published in Canada and distributed widely, and I suggest it would not be published were it not for the large fees that physicians have to pay in order to subscribe to it. I suggest it is read by very few doctors. It is of little value because of the fact the medical field has been split into so many specialties, and the Canadian market is so small no medical magazine in Canada has the resources to do the research work necessary to inform the medical field. By and large U.S. medical magazines are much wider read in Canada than the Canadian publication.
The $50 million or so spent by the National Research Council is largely lost because the results of research are not able to be published. The removal of these few magazines will further diminish the amount of medical knowledge that flows freely to Canada from throughout the world. This will make Canadian doctors even more cut off from the rest of the world.
In fact we have seen what has happened in the drug industry as a result of the passage of drug legislation a few years ago when potents were taken away from drug companies. Many drugs developed in the United States, in the United Kingdom, and in Europe are being marketed around the world, but in many cases there is little knowledge of these drugs in Canada. I suggest this is another result of drug legislation. With such programs as Parcost and provincial efforts to curtail drug prescriptions we have seen a reduction in the quality and certainly quantity of drugs being made available to the Canadian public. Advertising is extremely important to the drug trade. Many people think drugs are widely known throughout the world by all physicians, but that is not the fact. Most physicians learn about drugs through reading about them in medical journals and from details supplied by drug travellers.
One of the most widely read medical journals in this country is MD of Canada. Many drug companies advertise their products in this magazine, and the revenue from this advertising in large part allows the magazine to be printed. Most of these drug companies are based in Montreal. Without this advertising almost certainly the knowledge about new drugs would diminish substantially, and only the Canadian public is the loser.
Canadians have benefited more than most from medical discoveries throughout the world, and that is because most of the great discoveries are not made in Canada but in western Europe and in the United States. There is an enormous outpouring of medical knowledge from the United States which is freely available to the rest of the world. In fact our food and drug department does very

little but phone Washington and ask what is being done in respect of certain drugs that are being tested, and new drugs becoming available.
MD of Canada has a special place for people involved in medicine, and a special place as well for a small number of people who are not involved in the medical world. It is a very enriching magazine to its readers. It includes a written medical history that is extremely interesting, covering times from Julius Caesar, Napoleon and so on. This magazine is subscribed to almost exclusively by physicians so it is not in competition with any other journal or magazine. In fact there are no other magazines in which many of these companies can effectively advertise. The removal of these magazines from the Canadian market will in effect mean the end of this advertising.
Just a short time ago the Department of National Health and Welfare discontinued the practice, set up when the drug act was passed, of sending out selected drug information. Obviously the department felt that the bulk of this information ended up in the wastepaper baskets in doctors' offices.
Articles in MD of Canada are world-wide in scope, and many contain elements of history art, and music and their relationship to medicine. I have always appreciated the work of the originator of the magazine, Dr. Felix Marti Ibanez. Unfortunately he passed away at a very young age. He was the chief health officer of the Republic of Spain before the Franco civil war. That is probably equivalent to the position of deputy minister of health.
Modern Medicine, which is the corollary to MD of Canada, is also to be a casualty. Its value was in the fact that it contained condensations of many interesting articles from around the world. Thousands of medical articles are written but only a few can be read by any one individual. Modern Medicine has been a useful magazine in that it condenses many of these articles for the busy physician who does not have time to read extensively.
These magazines translate many of these world-wide articles into English so that doctors can take advantage of the information available. These articles are translated from Russian, Hindustani, French, Italian, Spanish and many other languages so that this information then becomes available to us. There is absolutely no possible substitution for these translations in this country, so again the information available to Canadian scientists will be restricted. I do not know what the point was in picking out these particular magazines.
Turning to the larger issue I should like to mention the CBC. I think the problem of the CBC is that it cannot stand some little competition. The CBC always attempts to inform the people what Canadians should do, think, and believe. But everywhere I go I notice that most radio and television sets seem to be tuned into American stations. What does this indicate? By and large it indicates that the CBC is not interesting. It is obvious when one listens to the CBC that it is trying to tell us something, that it is trying to lecture to us, or tell us we should do such and such a thing and should not buy this or should not do that. The CBC attempts to direct the public's morals. The CBC suffers because of this. When the CBC was established it

Instead of embarking on many of the things in which it is involved, the CBC would be doing much more for the country if it provided a minimum of television service to all parts of the country.
I feel this bill should be returned to the committee where we might hear what the sweetheart arrangement is between the government and Reader's Digest. I would hope we would hear what is the real meaning of a continuing relationship between Reader's Digest U.S.A. and Reader's Digest Canada, and why the same cannot be applied to Time Canada and Time U.S.A.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the third reading stage of the debate on Bill C-58, the bill which would end some of the income tax privileges for advertisers in non-Canadian magazines and also on nonCanadian television stations, I wish to make a few comments on behalf of the New Democratic Party.
We supported the legislation when it first came before the House. We saw it as long overdue. We have had some reservations concerning the interpretation by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) as it pertains to Reader's Digest, but on the whole we support the legislation and wish to see its passage at this time.
I really think my friends in the Conservative party are flogging a dead horse, a horse probably of their own creation, when they level charges of censorship and other kinds of wrongdoing at the government.
We debated this bill for months. It was first introduced over a year ago. The debate on second reading was prolonged mainly as a result of Conservative opposition. Very extensive hearings were held by the committee. The amendment before us to send the bill back to the committee seems to me to be a backward step which will not achieve anything.
In the committee we heard testimony from the officials of the Department of National Revenue concerning their interpretation of the 80 per cent different rule. I do not see how sending the bill back to the committee at this stage would further clarify that or in any way improve the bill.
It should be remembered that the main purpose of the bill is to promote a healthy Canadian periodical industry. Under the provisions of this bill the government will give tax advantages only to advertisers in bona fide Canadian magazines. The magazines must be 75 per cent Canadian-owned and they must not be substantially the same as a foreign parent magazine, which is defined as 80 per cent different. They also must not have an ongoing licensing arrangement with the parent company. Any magazine that fulfills those requirements by definition becomes a Canadian magazine and under the Income Tax Act their advertisers may deduct the cost of that advertising for income tax purposes.
In reality the bill before us provides an incentive to Canadian industry, in this case the magazine and television industry. I see nothing wrong with that principle. We have applied it to Canadian industry and manufacturing, and belatedly are applying it to the periodical industry in

recognition of its importance to the cultural, news, and information heritage of this country.
This bill is long overdue. Back in the early 1960's a royal commission recommended that unless we took this kind of action to sustain the Canadian publishing industry, this industry would slowly strangle from lack of advertising revenue as foreign magazines, mainly Time and Reader's Digest, set up branch plant operations in Canada and gained much of the advertising dollar. The government of that day, which happened to be a Conservative government, allowed an exemption for Time and Reader's Digest and a few other minor scholarly magazines, and said that for the purpose of income deduction for advertisers they would be classified as Canadian magazines. The consequence of that mistake, perpetuated by Liberal governments, is that today we find these two magazines, Time and Reader's Digest, have gained the lion's share of the advertising revenue, to the detriment of Canadian magazines.
I am not talking about Maclean's which is a healthy magazine but rather about many of the other small magazines which have been struggling to find a few advertising dollars which would make the difference between their continuing and expanding, or going under.
We have seen how the government has reacted to the tremendous lobby of Reader's Digest. It is estimated that in excess of $200,000 was spent on this lobby campaign with the general public and members of parliament. Indeed we have not for a long time seen such intensive lobbying on the Hill.
Tremendous pressure was placed on the Minister of National Revenue. They argued their case forcibly. They argued that theirs is a special case, that their magazine is a digest and therefore should be given some special consideration. We see this once again in terms of the minister allowing Reader's Digest to have access to a pool of original articles that the parent company collects. However, there is a condition, which we in this party accept, that if there is to be any editing or digesting it must be done by Canadian editors and that the going rate must be paid for any of the articles that are bought from the pool of the parent company. Of course they must also conform to Canadian ownership requirements.
I think that helps to allay many fears we had that somehow we were back in square one. The only criticism I have of that arrangement is that by virtue of the fact that the pool of articles that Reader's Digest Canada will choose from is a pool of articles decided by U.S. editors, in some roundabout way we could construct the argument that there is still a degree of editorial control in the United States. But the problem of course is that Reader's Digest in the United States has exclusive licensing arrangements with most major magazines, and therefore Reader's Digest Canada had to come to this kind of special arrangement with the Minister of National Revenue.
The only other thing that we see as a bit troublesome is the amount of discretion that the Minister of National Revenue has in determining how the act will apply to various magazines. We had hoped that this would be spelled out in more detail. However, this would mean major amendments to the Income Tax Act because that
February 23, 1976

discretionary power of course rests with the minister as it applies to other industries and individuals, and I do not see the government coming forward at this time with such amendments. So we had to accept the bill as it is, although it is imperfect to some degree in the areas that I mentioned.
We also support the bill because it seeks to end an outflow of advertising revenue to television stations, to the amount of some $20 million a year of Canadian advertising revenue which goes mainly to Buffalo stations and KVOS in Washington state, and hopefully then the advertisers would redirect these funds to Canadian television so that our stations can expand and produce more Canadian programming. In no way does the bill prohibit them from advertising on those stations just as in no way does it carry any degree of censorship provisions with respect to advertisers in magazines.
We support the bill. We have not put up many speakers because we saw the delaying tactics of our Conservative colleagues. They have aired the issue thoroughly, the Canadian people have had the chance to judge, and I believe that at this time the Canadian people want to see the bill passed. We are of that opinion in this party, and for that reason I urge my friends in the Conservative party, having put up the fight that they have, that they now accept the bill of the House so that we can get on with passing this piece of legislation and turn our attention to equally important legislation which lies ahead of us.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not anxious to take up too much of the time of the House but I do want to take a few minutes to express some views which I had mentioned back in November of last year regarding this bill, and in particular to support the amendment of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) that the bill be referred back to the committee for further study.
When I spoke on this issue in November of 1975 I was very concerned about the Canadian content portion of the bill. I never interpreted it as censorship. On the other hand, as I think I explained very clearly at the time, I interpreted it as editorial interference. At that time I made a case for certain scientific publications. There are a number involved in the medical area such as MD of Canada, Modern Medicine and Medical Aspects of Human Sexuality. I was somewhat concerned to find that there seems to have been some back room negotiations made with respect to Reader's Digest, while other periodicals were not given the same consideration.
I would like to think that there would be some recourse so that these periodicals or journals could be reassessed by the committee to see whether or not a formula could be devised to ensure their continued publication on the Canadian scene.
I should like to refer again to one of these periodicals of which I have a great deal of knowledge and which I have enjoyed over the years, that is, MD of Canada. I want to speak of it in particular because it is somewhat unique. As you know, the editor is Dr. Gibson who was invited to become the editor of that journal in April of 1973, following a great deal of searching on a world-wide context and following the death of the renowned Felix Marti Ibanez
Non-Canadian Publications
who was the founder and original editor of MD of Canada. As you know, Dr. Gibson is an internationally known physician and medical historian and he was a colleague of Dr. Ibanez.
When we look at MD of Canada it is important to realize that its own staff does the research and the writing and that the research and writing are done for physicians in the international context. We must remember that these are in-depth studies which add a great deal to the medical profession. I also want to point out that the news section is written by professional journalists. The head office is in Montreal. The medical news articles cover the major Canadian news of the day and meetings of various Canadian physicians.
I think that perhaps the most important thing about MD of Canada is that it is unique and that it has a humanistic concept which is not present in other medical journals with which I am familiar. It combines a cultural and historical interest greatly to the liking of physicians and professionals. If you look at MD of Canada and other medical journals you will find a striking difference. To quote Dr. Ibanez himself, he said it is the integration of medicine, society, and humanity translated editorially into a magazine of medical culture and cultural medicine.
I indicated some time ago that I have a very personal interest in this journal, and to try to demonstrate to the House the type of content found in the journal I had occasion earlier today to go back to some earlier publications of MD of Canada because, as I indicated previously, I had found some of these articles so interesting that I had kept them over the years.
As hon. members may know, I have a particular interest in the north and I would like to refer them to an excellent series of articles which appeared in the March, 1973, issue of MD of Canada. The cover story and feature article in that issue relates to the Arctic and is entitled "Arctic".
The lead article was written by Peter Freuchen. It is a fascinating, literary piece of writing and I should like to quote a little to give you some indication of the literary style of the journal:
You feel an undeniable sense of harmony as you stand listening to the beat of nature's heart, as your eyes penetrate endless horizons and your mind experiences a touch of eternity.
This article describes the Arctic very well. It goes into detail of the geophysics of the Arctic, the climatology of the Arctic, the flora of the Arctic, the population of the Arctic, and some of the recent developments in technology. I suggest that this kind of article is important in view of our interest in the recent developments in the northern part of Canada.
In this same issue of March, 1973, there is a superb article entitled "Icebound Nomads" about the Inuits and Eskimos, of whom there are 35,000 to 40,000 in the universe, about 10,000 of whom are in Canada.
There is another article which deals with the humanistic aspects of medicine and science combined. This article entitled "Polar Pioneer" is about the Norwegian Roald Amundsen and gives an excellent background of the Inuit

people not only in the Canadian context but in that of other countries.
A further article "Cold Comfort" describes the anthropological background of the Inuit people in northern Canada and northern Quebec. There are two more articles about the Arctic, which gives you some idea of the proportion of this magazine which was devoted to the Arctic. One article "Viking Beauty" related to art.
I want to stress that MD of Canada is a unique journal. Its editorial content is quite different from routine medical journals as we traditionally think of them. I have tried to impart to the House that the editorial attitude of MD of Canada is as universal as medicine itself. I indicated earlier that this concept was perceived by Dr. Marti Ibanez who was recognized internationally as a physician and humanitarian. This concept recognizes that physicians are members of an international medical community. Any other view of physicians would be too narrow, and the feature articles I have referred to reflect this concept. They attempt to combine the humanistic approach to man, his environment and, life style with the traditional reports on diseases. I emphasize that the literary component of the magazine is most important.
It should be recognized that the object of this journal is to stimulate medical culture, and this aspect of the magazine is unique. This is one of the reasons why I think it extremely important that the amendment before us be carried so that this specific publication can be reassessed by the committee.
Over the years I have found it interesting that lay persons are surprised that a magazine designed for the medical fraternity devotes such a share of editorial content to the arts or the humanities. These are the cornerstone of this particular journal, however. It is extremely important that the magazine be reassessed by the committee to see whether the same exception can be applied to it as has been applied to Reader's Digest.
The journal MD of Canada and the other MD magazines which I will refer to in a moment are really not designed for consumption just in Canada but for physicians everywhere. They are basically universal in nature and of interest to all physicians, whether they practice in the United States, Canada, Southeast Asia, Europe or wherever. Of course some of the articles touch on local aspects. In the ones I referred to, although they are international in context, a good deal of the information is based on experience in northern Canada, the Northwest Territories, northern Quebec and the Yukon territory-wherever the Inuit are found.
It is important to understand the MD concept. MD of Canada is no more a facsimile of MD, the medical news magazine of the United States than it is a facsimile of MD Espanola or any of the other international MD magazines. The complete editorial content of MD of Canada relates to the Canadian scene, and most of the news it covers is unavailable to Canadian physicians from any other single source. Reports or highlights of various medical and scientific meetings in Canada which are often not reported in other media are covered in MD of Canada. The "clinics" section deals with new findings in the international context. MD of Canada is the only source of this news which is so helpful to physicians in keeping abreast of problems in

today's fast moving world of medicine. The publication is sent to all physicians in Canada at no cost. The news section is different from what is contained in the United States edition or MD Espanola or the one that appears in southeast Asia.
From the beginning the magazine was published in Canada. It is important to remember this. It has been printed in Canada. The Canadian edition is not an edition printed outside and then brought into Canada. It is printed on Canadian paper, from typeset and plates manufactured in Canada, and mailed in Canada through the facilities of the Canadian Post Office, utilizing mailing lists provided by Canadian mailing houses. All advertising is solicited in Canada by the sales staff located in Montreal and in Oakville, Ontario.
I emphasize the importance of the free flow of medical information, regardless of its source. This free flow is essential to public health in this country and internationally. It should be considered as a magazine separate and distinct from any magazine published for the laity. MD of Canada has received favourable comments from thousands of physicians across this country, which illustrates the important contribution this important journal is making to the practice of medicine. It is doing this by supplying information of medical value, of value, I might say, to physicians around the world. I emphasize that the exchange of scientific information internationally is most important and I find unacceptable any curtailment of the international exchange of scientific information, or flow of scientific information to those interested in scientific ventures.
To sum up, MD of Canada is a controlled circulation magazine without subscriptions or revenue. Paid circulation magazines might choose to send non-Canadian editions to Canada, for sale to readers. That choice is not open to MD of Canada. Its only revenue source is advertising. If this important medical publication, which has been sent to this country's physicians for more than 15 years, were to cease publication in Canada as a result of Bill C-58, our medical profession would be the losers. The magazine could not be replaced, in the Canadian context.
I repeat that MD of Canada is not a Canadian edition of a foreign magazine. It is not a split run edition magazine; neither is it sold here as part of the overflow circulation of a parent magazine. It is a fully integrated Canadian medical publication which publishes material of value to the medical profession. It warrants repeating and emphasizing that the magazine's concept, its viewpoint, is important. It is unique in the field of medical journalism. It combines humanism, art, culture, and medicine.
MD of Canada purchases its typesetting, printing, labelling and mailing services in Canada. By definition, MD of Canada is a magazine of medical culture, and of cultural medicine, as I have emphasized. It carries a completely Canadian medical news section.

If this bill is in the wrong direction and based on unsound principles we are going to oppose it. It has been demonstrated that the opposition got results with the length of debates. You know, Madam Speaker, this is narrow nationalism; it is cheap nationalism. Actually some of the arguments used to justify this bill are not worthy of a banana republic. But some forget that this sort of thing is a two-way street.

None of the operation would be carried out in Canada. Not even the Post Office would get anything out of it, not a blessed cent. Somehow a face-saving has been found for Reader's Digest. I am going to ask, what was the deal? Was it the pressure of government backbenchers that caused the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) and the cabinet to modify the strictures and restrictions of the Cullen rule and certainly that new minister's interpretation of his powers and what he would do to whip everybody into line?
Let us have Reader's Digest tell the members of the committee what promise they got from the government. I am not unhappy. I am not criticizing Reader's Digest. I think they acted properly to save employment and revenues for Canada with regard to income tax, postal service and so on.
A tremendous amount of the cost of publishing Reader's Digest, both French and English versions, will remain in Canada for the benefit of Canadians. It was going to be thrown out, totally. What saved it? Surely the members of this House are entitled to an explanation.
When they appeared before the committee the representatives of Reader's Digest said they could not live with the restrictions in this bill. The government was obdurate. The net result was that Reader's Digest was going to go. Now there is a deal. It is owed to this House by the government and Reader's Digest to furnish the explanation.

As I was saying, I want to find out the arrangement with Reader's Digest. That being out, what about Time Canada? I have no particular brief with regard to the content of Time Canada. Some people pretend that that magazine should contain more Canadian news. When I look at the average issue of Time, even the United States edition, and considering that the United States has ten times the population and a great deal more activity around the world, proportionately I think that Canada gets more space than does the United States on the world scene. To that extent the suggestion that Canada should rate more coverage in a world-wide magazine is unrealistic.
I am looking now at the new format of Macleans. There is a lot more Canadian news. It is not world news. It is Canadian, shall we say local, events. I am not complaining about that. It always struck me that Macleans magazine existed mainly for the benefit of the Toronto school of writers, the "in" group. The editorship seemed to move around like musical chairs. They all praise one another. It was a self-serving operation. They may not like what I have to say, but I should like something to break that up. They don't supply a substitute at all. I don't suppose they really need to supply a substitute on a world-wide basis.
If Canadians are restricted to reading Time magazine as it will be brought in from the United States, the postal revenue will, of course, be lost. Printing revenues will be lost. All the effort and materials which go into Time

Canada will be totally lost to us. Mr. Speaker, there is such a thing as cutting off one's nose to spite one's face and in this action on the part of the government we are witnessing the same sort of thing. If it wants to encourage Canadian publications let it do so by all means, but not by the regressive and repressive methods proposed in Bill C-58.
I heartily endorse the amendment put forward by my hon. friend from Surrey-White Rock. I also submit that if the government and the New Democratic Party are unwise enough to reject it and draw a veil of secrecy over the whole situation, the House would be well advised to reject the bill entirely. This is bad legislation operating entirely on a false premise. If you apply to other nations the same principles as are applied here you would deny the operations of many Canadians abroad. There is no logic in this approach, and I consider that the minister's recommendation in favour of this legislation should be entirely rejected.
