speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to say a few words about this bill I must admit I have not been studying it as carefully as I might have done during the last few days. This is because I have had some other things on my mind and I hope they are reported in the Canadian edition of Time magazine when it comes out in the coming week. I look forward to seeing its comments on the leadership convention which has just concluded.
I support the amendment to send this bill back to committee. I am concerned about the deal made with Reader's Digest. I rose to speak on this matter originally because of the many letters and representations I received from constituents who feared that the Digest would no longer be delivered in their mail boxes. To their relief they find that some deal has been made which will allow Reader's Digest to continue as a Canadian publication.
I sympathize to some extent with the feelings of those who desire to encourage a sense of Canadian nationalism. The problem about this bill is the 80 per cent content rule, and this was the subject of a great deal of discussion which went on in the committee. I do not believe governments should become involved in deciding what the content should be of any magazine in this country.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) discussing MD of Canada. He told us that this was a staff-researched and staff-written publication and that all these articles were researched and written for physicians in Canada. He pointed out that the editorial content reflected a unique humanism which combined the cultural and historical interests of the physician with his professional interests. This was the striking difference between MD of Canada and other medical publications. I recall recently reading one of the articles in MD of Canada. It concerned the life of one of the wives of King Henry VIII, Anne Boleyn, and the reasons for her various medical problems. This article was of great interest to me, as I am sure it was to a great many people.
We all know there is a great deal of unemployment in the country at the present time. If we force these publications out of Canada, jobs will be lost. The rate of unemployment, now running at about 7 per cent, is of such concern to me that I believe the effect of the bill upon the employment situation will in itself be a basic consider-
February 23, 1976

ation. I do not believe we encourage Canadian magazines by restricting the content they are allowed to print.
In the last few weeks I have been talking to many of my constituents about this bill. I find they have been reading about it in the press. Some have been reading Hansard. And people are still confused. Some believe we are subsidizing Reader's Digest by giving that publication special tax considerations. Others say we are not. Some people are asking whether we did offer both -Time and the Digest special concessions at some time or another. Having regard to this situation I suggest we spend a little longer on this legislation, send it back to the committee and discuss the arrangements which exist as between the government and these publications.
I am also concerned, as an agronomist, lest various magazines of interest to my profession may be restricted by the legislation before us. I listened with interest to what the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) had to say about publications in the field of agriculture. He suggested that livestock advertisements might be covered by the bill and that the results might adversely affect Canadian farmers trying to sell livestock in the United States and elsewhere.
For all these reasons I felt I should enter the debate to-night to lend my support to the amendment of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock which seeks to send the bill back to committee for further study so the committee can deal with a number of considerations raised by many hon. members during the debate in this House.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISIONS ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great misfortune that apparently the minister and some of his backers do not see fit to think about some matters that are of fundamental importance to the Canadian people. I refer to freedom-economic freedom, freedom of the press, and freedom of worship. These are the three basic freedoms on which this country has been built. They have meant much to Canadians of all races and creeds, but apparently they mean little to the minister and those who support him.
I have a great deal of respect for members on the government side of the House who disagree strenuously with the minister about the legislation he has presented to the House. I agree wholeheartedly with the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy), who suggested that it would be well to take a portion of the CBC's budget to assist publishers in this country. The waste of the CBC would probably never be noticed since its budget is so large. When the hon. member for Timmins asked why we should not give 10 per cent of the CBC's budget to the publishers who would then have more money than they can ever hope to gain from all of the Time and Reader's Digest advertising, he raised a point of fundamental importance. If we were to do that, or something like it, there would not be the fear of this legislation that exists on this side of the House.
The fear that we have is related to interpretation. We have gone over this and I hope that the minister will eventually take heed of the matters with which we are greatly concerned. Section 19.1 specifically states that "in computing income no deduction shall be made in respect of an otherwise deductible outlay or expense of a taxpayer
Non-Canadian Publications
made or incurred for an advertisement directed primarily to a market in Canada". This is where this question of interpretation comes into focus and it is why the amendment of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) should be passed and the bill sent back to committee. The minister should tell the committee exactly what he means when he uses the phrase "advertisement directed primarily".
I have been in contact with some of the officials in the Department of National Revenue and they do not know the answer to that question. I should like to know whether or not the minister knows, and I feel the committee has the right to ask that fundamental question.
It has been suggested that ample time has been given when the legislation went to committee. I am sure you are very much aware, Mr. Speaker, having been chairman of parliamentary committees, that when five minutes is offered a member of a committee to question the minister, and he perhaps has only that one opportunity during the meeting, he can only touch on the outer parameters of his questions before his time expires. Some other member of the committee continues his questioning on other aspects, and as a result not sufficient time is given for the questioning that should take place in connection with a very fundamental principle of Canadian democracy, freedom of the press.
We have seen what happens when freedom of the press is lost. With today's communications it might be said that the world is becoming smaller. We can no longer live unto ourselves alone. Many governments are run on socialistic lines; we even have socialists in this House. However, governments that do not mind interfering with freedoms have no reservations about taking them away from individuals and allowing government, or governmental officials, to make decisions. Communism began in Russia, moved into China, into southern Asia, then into South America and now into Africa. Our North American continent remains relatively free of governmental control.
I think you would agree with me, Mr. Speaker, being the honourable man that you are, that we should protect this principle of freedom to our last drop of blood. Let no one interfere with our freedoms even though they are being eroded away one by one, principle by principle, in other countries. It may not be long before we too have none left.
As I said earlier, we have our basic freedoms-economic freedom, freedom of speech, and freedom of worship. Whether the legislative controls under which we now have to live are good or bad is beside the point. They are nevertheless controls, and once controls are put in place it is very difficult to get rid of them. We have found that out from experience. We all remember that income tax was supposed to be a temporary control. It was introduced many years ago, yet it is still with us and has quite an impact on society today. As I say, if these regulations are put into place they will be very difficult to remove.
Governments in Canada of one form or another are spending 40 cents of every dollar of our gross national product. In other words, 40 per cent of our economic freedom has disappeared. We do not know how long this will continue. I point out that in some socialist countries today the percentage is 70 or 80 per cent. Certainly I hope this

February 23, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
country can put on the brakes quickly and firmly enough so we do not find ourselves in the same position.
So it is with our other freedom, freedom of the press. Why should we allow a minister or a member of his department to interpret what constitutes Canadian content? I do not think anyone in this House of Commons, however intelligent he may be, could adequately define what Canadian content is in all situations and on all occasions. I think that is an absolute impossibility. Why then should we give this authority to a minister? I see no reason in the world why we should do that, and certainly not because the tax dollars we are speaking about are a very small or minute portion of the total tax dollars, or small in relation to our gross national product. The minister certainly is not playing fair with government members, members on this side of the House, or the Canadian public, and I have to take exception to that situation.
I pay honour to those members on the government side who feel about this bill as we do on this side. Let me spend a little bit of time in support of what the hon. member for Timmins has said. That hon. member suggested that this bill does not present any extensive degree of censorship. The hon. member referred to "extensive degree", but he then went on to say that there is a degree of censorship. Why should we allow any individual to propose censorship or control in respect of what Canadian people wish to read?
The hon. member then went on to say that the argument regarding the lack of legal authority of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) or the abuse of it has been overdone. I cannot agree with him in that, because I think the minister has not been flexible enough in this legislation. The only flexibility shown by the Minister of National Revenue was in respect of the provision for Reader's Digest. He made a change which allowed Reader's Digest a place in the Canadian plan of things.
The point I am trying to impress upon the House is that we have the right to know why and on what basis the minister decided it was in the best interests of the government to make this decision in respect of Reader's Digest. Unfortunately under the rules of the House, of which you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, we are not allowed to question policies or the reasons for legislation now before the House. We all recognize this rule and try to abide by it. However, this does create problems in certain situations such as the one we are dealing with at the present time, because we cannot ask the minister why and on what basis he changed his policy. This could be done in the committee, and that is why it is of fundamental importance that the bill be sent back to the committee where we can question the minister, and perhaps call further witnesses. Perhaps representatives of Reader's Digest would also have something to say in respect of this change in the legislation.
The hon. member for Timmins went on to say, and this is very important, that the answer and the reasonable position lay somewhere in the middle between what the minister is suggesting and what we on this side are proposing. I think it is reasonable to expect the minister to show some flexibility. Up to the present time he has not done so.

The hon. member for Timmins went on to suggest that the minister and the government have never accepted the consideration of any middle ground position, and considering the type of mild amendments which have been refused by the government, even amendments that would have been useful without detracting to any degree from the bill, then he felt that the minister was operating from a point of total inflexibility and maybe even from bad will. Why should we in this House of Commons have to deal with inflexibility of this nature? It would seem to me that at some time the minister should stand and state unequivocally what was involved in this change he he made for Reader's Digest.
The hon. member for Timmins then went on to say it might well be that the Minister of National Revenue and his officials will look the other way when a Canadian publication is involved and that, indeed, if the government could wring out of its interpretation an accommodation for Reader's Digest it could certainly wring one out for a Canadian publisher. However, the fact remains that our Canadian publishers will have to face this legislation always, and it may be that they will be hurt by it while it may not necessarily hurt foreign publications.
Before this bill receives third reading I hope the minister will stand in his place and tell us exactly what happened that resulted in this change of interpretation. I hope he will tell us exactly what happened between his former position and the one he is now maintaining. This is of fundamental importance because there are other magazines involved.
I proposed an amendment to this House which was rejected, I must say to my regret. That amendment was referred to by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schel-lenberger). It had reference to foreign owned magazines which aimed their advertisement at the Canadian market. As I said earlier, this world is becoming smaller, and surely there should and could be an arrangement whereby the United States and Canada could benefit from magazines published in each country. We both have much to gain by a common understanding and a common purpose. There is not much difference between their thinking and ours. Their well being is closely associated with ours, and to a great degree our philosophies are the same. If we could have an interchange of ideas and thoughts surely it would be to our mutual benefit.
One other matter of concern to me is in respect of research. We heard from officials of the Department of Agriculture that research is falling badly behind because we are unable to keep up with technical change. One official went on to say that much research is being done in the field because the department is falling behind in research at headquarters.
It would seem mutually beneficial to all concerned if we had exchange of information back and forth across the 49th parallel. We all realize that many of our magazines received in Canada are published in the United States.
It was my privilege for some time to serve as the superintendent of a Presbyterian Sunday school organization, and I have no hesitancy in telling you about this. There are a great many people who belong to that church, but they are still not in a position to publish their own Sunday school material. In view of the fact that we must rely on
February 23, 1976

American publications for the edification of our pupils to a great degree, why in the world can we not have a mutual understanding between the two countries as we have between the two church bodies?
According to this legislation if an organization, a corporation or whatever, wished to advertise in a magazine directed to the Canadian market it would not be eligible to have that advertising expense treated as a deduction for income tax purposes. I think this is wrong. I believe we actually are dealing with peanuts so far as the government is concerned, but it certainly is not peanuts when one considers the church organizations which must depend on public support for their sustenance. I should like to hear the minister tell us whether this legislation is actually aimed at this type of advertiser or publication. Surely this is not the case, because sometime he also will die and I am sure he would want to know where he is going. I believe many people at this point in time would like to tell him where to go, and where to take this legislation.
We must realize that this matter is of fundamental importance. Many letters have been received from people involved. No doubt down the road there may be other innocent bystanders who will be caught up in this. Surely the minister could give this further consideration because of the fact that it is open for interpretation.
As I suggested before, the minister basically is a good fellow. Many of us are prepared to trust him because of the fact that he has proven that he is trustworthy, but what guarantee can he give us that he will always be in that position? He cannot give that guarantee. What guarantee can he give that the present government will always be the government? I hope it is not and I do not believe it will be.
If the time should ever come when we have in Canada a government that has no hesitancy in taking away the freedoms of the people then certainly it would not be very difficult for a person, a minister, or a government to change the interpretation. We must realize that interpretation is one of the significant factors involved. That is the reason why there are so many church groups in the world of today. Interpretations differ. So many people interpret the basic philosophy in a different manner.
In the realization that this is a matter of interpretation and relevancy I find this legislation to be abhorrent. I would hope the minister would stand up in his place and say he would agree to accept this amendment, take the legislation back to the committee and thereby give the committee an ample opportunity to quiz the minister, and perhaps hear further witnesses because of the fact that I do not think they have had a full opportunity to present their case adequately to the committee.

subtopic: HOUSING-ALLEGATION OWNER OF 800 RICHMOND ST. WEST, TORONTO, CHARGED RENTS HIGHER THAN AUTHORIZED
HOUSING-ALLEGATION OWNER OF 800 RICHMOND ST. WEST, TORONTO, CHARGED RENTS HIGHER THAN AUTHORIZED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, February 18, I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) the following question:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that an owner of a limited dividend building located at 800 Richmond Street West in Toronto charged tenants of two-bedroom apartments in the building $189 a month in February, 1975, and increased the rent to $205 commencing in February 1976, whereas the rental agreement between CMHC and the owner of the building stipulates that the rent be $173.25, will the minister direct CMHC to have the owner return the over-payments to the tenants forthwith, and not to permit any increase in rent until CMHC and the landlord have negotiated a new rent increase based on actual cost to the landlord?
I thought the Minister of State for Urban Affairs was * prepared to answer the question at that time but the Speaker thought there was too much detail and did not permit the question.
May I review with you very shortly and quickly the details. There is an owner of a limited dividend project at 800 Richmond Street West in Toronto who entered into an agreement with CMHC, and as of February, 1975, the agreement called for rent of $173.25 for a two bedroom apartment, but the landlord of that building charged the tenants not $173.25 but $189. Then in February of 1976 the landlord charged the tenants $205. If you look at those increases in rent you will note that the first rent instead of being $173.25 was $189, an overpayment of $15.75 a month or $189 a year, and the second increase to $205 amounts to an overcharge of $31.75 a month, or $381 a year.
What the landlord has done regarding rents in one bedroom or three bedroom apartments in the building I do not know, but for two bedroom apartments he certainly has overcharged. When the tenants became aware of this overcharge they contacted CMHC which said to them that they can take the problem to the Ontario Rent Review Board or, if the landlord does not repay these overcharges, they might call in the mortgage because of the breach.
What should CMHC have done in these circumstances, and I am assuming that the facts are correct because I received them from responsible people? Surely what they should have done is to order immediate repayment to the tenants of the overpayment to the landlord, and if the landlord failed to make the repayment they should have taken immediate legal steps with regard to the breach of the legal contract.
However, there is a bigger issue in this problem than the overcharging of rents, and that is the role of tenants concerning agreements entered into between CMHC and the owners of limited dividend buildings. Last summer the Minister of State for Urban Affairs met with representatives of the Metro Federation of Limited Dividend Tenants and they asked for three main items to be discussed. One was standards of maintenance in limited dividend projects, the second was a grievance procedure with regard to problems they would have concerning the building, and the third was participation by the tenants in discussions and negotiations between CMHC and the landlord. These are reasonable requests but to date I have heard nothing, and

neither have they, from the minister with regard to these problems.
Surely the tenants have the right to have knowledge of the basic terms of the agreement entered into between CMHC and the landlord. When I talk about the basic terms I mean the rent, the maintenance, and the terms of the contract, because with regard to rent under the Anti-Inflation Act and with regard to the limitation imposed by the Ontario government they are only entitled to costs such as increased taxes, heating, electricity, maintenance and insurance increases. If the tenants are forced to pay increases they should know what these actual costs are so that they can determine whether these costs are right and reasonable in the circumstances.
The agreement between CMHC and the landlord should not be a secret document; it should be a public document, and the tenants of CMHC buildings, both in limited dividend projects and public housing projects, should get a summary of agreements entered into between CMHC and the landlord so that they know just what the rent is, what the term is, and what other terms affect them.
With regard to the limited dividend projects, the moneys that are applied to mortgage financing are public moneys. Surely the tenants should have the right to know what the problems are. I am rather shocked that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs has not taken the initiative to publicize the terms of the limited dividend agreements entered into between the landlord and CMHC.
I look forward to the answer of the parliamentary secretary. He is a reasonable person and I am sure he has documented the problem and will give a good answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-ALLEGATION OWNER OF 800 RICHMOND ST. WEST, TORONTO, CHARGED RENTS HIGHER THAN AUTHORIZED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond on behalf of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) who is currently on a very important mission to Africa and the Middle East, where he is meeting with various heads of state for the purpose of discussing participation in Habitat, the United Nations Conference on Human Settlements, to be held later this year in Vancouver. Knowing the hon. member's strongly held humanitarian views on proper housing and living conditions, I know he will be a vigorous supporter of that conference.
With regard to the question he has raised tonight, it is gratifying to have the hon. member support the minister's efforts to provide reasonably priced rental accommodation for Canadians.
I think the minister would agree with him also that we should look into the three points he raised with regard to the standard of maintenance, grievance procedures, and participation by tenants. I will look into them and see if anything can be brought forward and if the hon. member and I can continue studying these matters.
As to the specific case the hon. member has described to the House, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is currently reviewing the developer's operating costs for 800 Richmond Street West, Toronto, in order to decide what level of rents is appropriate. The building was financed under section 15 of the National Housing Act, where an operating agreement between the developer and CMHC forms a part of the mortgage. The terms of the agreement
February 23, 1976

make provision for a review of operating costs when the developer requests an increase in rents. If the agreement is violated, the corporation may institute foreclosure action, or seek other remedies through the courts under the agreement. It should be pointed out, however, that CMHC does not have the power to direct the owner to make refunds of payments in excess of the authorized rents. The minister expects to have the results of the CMHC investigation by the time he returns from his trip. I am sure he will advise the hon. member and the House of his conclusion.
I appreciate the hon. member's remarks on the other points he made. I shall take them up with the minister and try to get some answers to the problems.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PENSIONS FOR FORMER PRISONERS OF WAR-POSITION OF MINISTER IF CABINET FAILS TO SUPPORT MEASURE
VETERANS AFFAIRS-PENSIONS FOR FORMER PRISONERS OF WAR-POSITION OF MINISTER IF CABINET FAILS TO SUPPORT MEASURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Railton) in the House. I was hoping the minister could stay but I am sure he is quite busy.
I raised a question on the legislation that was promised to provide compensation for prisoners of war on the basis of the length of time they were incarcerated. On January 28 the minister indicated that he would make an announcement, probably within two weeks. On further questioning by myself and by my colleagues, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles), the word was always the same, the problem was being considered in cabinet. Mr. Speaker, I wish they would take that word consideration out of the English language. It appears the only answers we ever get are that the matter "is under consideration".
On February 13 the minister replied again that it was being considered by cabinet and the House leader, who seems to support the procrastination in cabinet to deny these veterans, promised me a long outstanding date which is now overdue. I do not know what they are waiting for. The amounts involved are insignificant, particularly compared with next year's spending estimates of $42 billion. One wonders why nothing is done. One can only presume that the government is leaning on the backs of veterans in restraining its spending.
According to figures I have, $2.3 million could be spent on Japanese theatre prisoners of war, and $6.7 million on other prisoners of war, making a total of about $9 million. A number of former prisoners of war have passed on, which will probably reduce that total by $1 million. I see, from looking at the new estimates, that spending under the veterans land administration, legislation which was phased out against the wishes of veterans, is to be reduced from $13 million to $9 million. If the parliamentary secretary wants to know where extra money can be found, surely the government could use the $4 million it saved for the benefit of prisoners of war.
The members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs have supported the minister, as have the veterans.
Adjournment Debate
We all think, with due respect, that he has brought in good legislation, and introduced many improvements to existing legislation, which we have supported. But, as he himself says, so long as veterans are alive, we shall need improvements in legislation, if only to cope with veterans' needs.
Inflation being what it is today, it is obvious that veterans' allowances and disability pensions are not keeping up with the increase in the cost of living. The Canadian Labour Congress brought this to the minister's attention. It showed that some veterans on war veterans allowance are getting less than they would get if they earned even the minimum wage. Inflation today is badly hurting our five million poverty-stricken people. Statistics Canada figures show that a family of two needs a minimum of $5,000 today to survive. So it is obvious that there is a need to increase pensions and war veterans allowances.
I mention this because I want to draw attention to those prisoners of war who were incarcerated for up to two and a half years. The Hermann report mentions the pre-aging process. The parliamentary secretary, who is very capable and served with distinction as a medical officer, realizes the effect of incarceration on prisoners of war, even at this late date.
It is now four years since the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs recommended that the plight of former prisoners of war be studied and the Hermann report commissioned. We, on my side of the House, want to know facts. Let the parliamentary secretary say, either yes, or no, will legislation be introduced soon. Today in the House when answering the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the minister indicated that probably in a week he would have the answer for us. He told me on January 28 he would know the answer in two weeks. He said much the same today. Does his answer of today mean we must wait one week, two weeks or three weeks? The question is, how long must veterans wait.
It is an insult when the minister says that the matter is "under consideration". We have supported his position in cabinet. The Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs is not partisan. We understand the situation, and the minister's position in the government, and we want a yes or no answer: can we expect the legislation soon; or, when can we expect it? We need to know, to allay the fears and concerns of veterans across the country who expect the legislation and look forward to it, because it was promised. Hopefully the parliamentary secretary this evening will give us the answer to our question, and say that the minister will announce a date by next Friday.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-RESTORATION OF RAIL SERVICE TO GLENWOOD AND HILL SPRING-REASON FOR DELAY
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-RESTORATION OF RAIL SERVICE TO GLENWOOD AND HILL SPRING-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just cannot believe that the minister did not see fit to be in the House tonight or at least to appoint somebody. Oh, I see he has appointed someone.
On November 7, November 18, November 21, December 2, January 28, and January 29 I directed questions to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in an effort to have a railway bridge repaired in Glenwood and Hill Spring which was damaged by floods in June, 1975. On November 7 I asked the following question:
In light of the fact that the CPR informed me over four months ago that a bridge would be provided in the Glenwood-Hill Spring area in order to facilitate the movement of grain, and in light of the fact that this has not even been started, will the minister assure the House that every effort will be made to have this situation corrected immediately?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I think there may be a requirement and a role for the Canadian Transport Commission in relation to the bridge on this particular line, but I will look into the matter.
On November 18 I asked the following question:
In answer to my question in this House on November 7 regarding restoration of rail service to Glenwood and Hill Spring, the minister informed me there may be a requirement and a role for the Canadian Transport Commission. Since that time the CPR has notified Mr. Harold Boucher, President of the Chamber of Commerce in Magrath, that it is awaiting word from the CTC. Would the minister inform the House where the confusion lies, since the CPR says the bridge has to be restored in order to provide service?
The minister replied:
-we have been considering the question of the use of trucks immediately to move grain from that area, and some steps are going forward toward this end.
I then asked the following supplementary question:
In view of the fact the minister has stated that the bridge has to be repaired, would he inform the House why the CPR hauled 15 loads over the bridge but now refuses to haul any more and has cut off service to people in the area?
The minister replied:
I am not sure at which stage the hon. member refers to the materials having been hauled. As I understand it, the bridge is not safe for service and therefore cannot be used to provide service in the ordinary course.
On November 21 I asked the minister the following:
In light of the fact that at a meeting held in Magrath, Alberta in November of 1972 the ex-minister of agriculture, Mr. Olson, informed the meeting that "If any producer suffered any loss due to inability to deliver grain as a result of plugged elevators, CP rail would be responsible", would the minister inform the House whether or not he has instructed the CPR to restore service to Glenwood and Hillspring?
The minister's answer was:
I rather think the former minister of agriculture's words have been taken out of context. The question of restoration of service is one, as I have said before, that depends on certain action on the part of the CTC.
In my supplementary I asked:
In view of the fact that the Minister of Transport has informed me that he has to get a hold of the CTC, that the CTC has told me they have to get a hold of the CPR, and that the CPR has told me they have to get a hold of the Minister of Transport, would the minister please inform the House how I go about restoring service?
And this was the minister's answer:
As I told the hon. member earlier, we are all trying to get a hold of each other.
Next, Mr. Speaker, I quote my question of December 2.
On November 21 the minister received a telegram from the Chamber of Commerce in Magrath as follows:
Advise what arrangements made to move grain from Glenwood and Hillspring elevator. Situation desperate. Grain piled on ground. Deteriorating daily. Surely you can order CP Rail to move grain either by rail or truck.
Again, this was the answer:
Any such instructions would have to originate from the CTC. The problem with grain movement is that there is difficulty with a bridge that can handle ordinary service. There is real doubt about the ability of anyone to order a movement by truck. However, we have been negotiating toward a specific truck movement of grain. We are attempting to put the final details of that movement in place. I hope to be able to tell these communities in short order about that plan.
On January 28 I put my next question as follows:
On November 7, 18 and 21 I asked the minister questions regarding the restoration of rail service to Glenwood and Hill Spring and the minister replied in part on one occasion that the CTC had a part to play in the matter, a bridge was under repair and that the CTC, CPR and the Minister of Transport were all looking for one another. Will the minister inform the House whether or not he plans to do anything about this serious situation?
To which the minister replied:
I will check the exact dates on which certain steps were taken in this regard and bring the hon. member up to date on the matter.
On January 29, in the course of a further question, I said:
There is to be a meeting of the Chamber of Commerce in Glenwood tonight to discuss methods which might be used to restore grain transportation. Will the minister assure the House that he will contact the Chamber of Commerce in Glenwood before their meeting tonight with a statement of his intentions?
This the minister did as promised. I should like to read a telegram which was later sent to the minister as follows:

February 23, 1976

Our executive express sincere appreciation your wire January 29 advising you had requested president Canadian Pacific Railway to immediately repair bridge Cardston Glenwood Line. Have they agreed to do so and when may we expect normal service? Advise.
As of this point in time Mr. Boucher has not been advised of anything. The trucks are not moving grain. The bridge has not been repaired. I just wonder what the answer will be tonight. Will it be that the CPR tenders are let and that an announcement is forthcoming? Will it be the trucks are too expensive? Will it be that nobody wants to work? I think the CPR has been the scapegoat for the Minister of Transport.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-RESTORATION OF RAIL SERVICE TO GLENWOOD AND HILL SPRING-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the name of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) I would like to tell the hon. member I hope to be able to satisfy him with an answer tonight. Before getting to the heart of the answer I should like to summarize briefly the event which caused the disruption of the CP Rail Cardston subdivision run from Stirling through Cardston to Glenwood, some 73 miles.
Last summer a flash flood damaged a bridge, cutting the line west of Cardston to Glenwood and isolating two elevators at Hill Spring-two primary elevators with a capacity of 160,000 bushels-and Glenwood where there are four primary elevators with a total capacity of 250,000 bushels.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-RESTORATION OF RAIL SERVICE TO GLENWOOD AND HILL SPRING-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext: I already know that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-RESTORATION OF RAIL SERVICE TO GLENWOOD AND HILL SPRING-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext:
This incident caused 15 rail cars to be marooned by the flood between Cardston and Glenwood. Immediately reacting to this situation it
Adjournment Debate
was possible to winch rail cars one at a time across the bridge. Evidently the ministries concerned did not stop there. We carried out an initial examination of the various alternative means of restoring service and their respective cost elements. This examination indicated that trucking the grain out from these two elevators would be preferable to rebuilding the bridge, bearing in mind this is one of the lines which is being looked at by the Hall Commission whose report is expected by the end of the 1976.
A closer examination of the costs proved that the truck option was higher than the initial indication, because if all the grain were trucked out to Cardston it would create congestion problems at Cardston. Also, trucking distances to the alternate delivery points of Brocket and Fort MacLeod would be greater and would be over roads that have severe load limitations during certain times of the year. Furthermore, the trucking option would involve a second elevation with increased costs.
The higher than anticipated trucking costs caused us to ask the Canadian Transport Commission to carry out a full study of the various rail options. On the basis of the CTC study it became evident that it was preferable to rebuild the bridge at an estimated cost of $75,000. On January 30 the Minister of Transport wrote to Mr. Burbidge, president of the CPR, and asked CP rail to rebuild the bridge. Canadian Pacific rail has agreed and confirmed that in fact construction crews were already on site and CP rail estimated that reconstruction would be completed in approximately six weeks.
